Return and Rehabilitation of Kashmiri Migrants 
*302.   SHRI RAJEEV SHUKLA:  
            DR. ABRAR AHMED:† 
Will the Minister of HOMEFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a)  whether any Action Plan for the return and rehabilitation of Kashmiri 
migrants have been prepared; and 
(b) if so, the status of the plan? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS 
(SHRI HARIN PATHAK): (a) and (b) A statement is laid on the Table of the 
House. 
Statement 
(a) and (b) In order to enable safe and honourable return of migrants to their 
native places in the Valley, the then State Government of J&K had finalized 
an Action Plan involving a total amount of Rs. 2589.73 crores. The Union 
Government has agreed to reimburse costs borne by tha State Government as 
per approved norms in the case of those 
†The question was actually asked on the floor of the House by Dr. Abrar Ahmed. 
 
 
    1

RAJYA SABHA [12 March, 2003] 
Kashmiri migrants who actually return to the Valley.The Action Plan is to be 
implemented in phases which envisages return and rehabilitation of migrant 
families in areas where clusters of migrant houses are available and in 
villages/mohallas in the Kashmir Valle y Districts with sizeable Kashmiri 
Pandit population and where security is already being provided. To begin 
with, 166 houses forming 15 clusters were identified in Srinagar and Badgam 
Districts, which are considered safe for the return of the owners of these 
houses. The list of these clusters was published in the newspapers and steps 
were taken to identify the families and find their willingness to return to their 
homes. About 50 families who were registered with the Relief organisation, 
Jammu were contacted personally to give their consent for return to the 
Valley on the basis of the package announced by the Government. Interaction 
meetings with some of these families were also held but as reported by State 
Government, only two families (not belonging to the particular area) have 
agreed to return to the valley so far. 
The new State Government has indicated that it has identified the shrines 
in Mattan and Kheer Bhavani where the Kashmiri migrants displaced from 
these places could be settled temporarily by developing two model clusters 
containing temporary shelters for Kashmiri migrants, till such time they can 
repair their existing residential houses. Ministry of Finance has agreed to 
provide a grant of Rs. 10 crores to the State Government for the 
reconstruction/renovation of houses and shrines at Kheer Bhavani and 
Mattan.

Crimes against women 
*303.   DR.T. SUBBARAMI REDDY:† 
            SHRIMATI SHABANA AZMI: 
Will the Minister of HOME AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether in the year 2002, there had been increasing number of crimes 
against women; 
†The question was actually asked on the floor of the House by Dr. T. Subbarami Reddy. 
5 

RAJYA SABHA [12 March, 2003] 
(b) if so, what were the main reasons for the same; 
(c) what are the efforts being made to reduce these crimes against women 
in 2003; 
 
(d) whether any proposals in this regard have been worked out; and 
(e) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS 
(SHRI I.D. SWAMI): (a) to (e) A statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) The incidence of crime committed against women as reported in 
2000 were 1,41,373 which increased to 1,43,866 during 2001, thereby 
registering an increase of 1.8% during 2001 over 2000. 
(b) Poverty, work participation, social practices like dowry, the absence 
of gender sensitization, anonymity in urban areas and the physical vulnerability of 
women are some of the reasons for crime against women. 
(c) to (e) 'Police' and 'Public Order' are State subjects. Prevention of all 
crime including crime against women is primarily the responsibility of the 
State Governments. However, Government of India has been advising the 
State Governments from time to time to improve the administration of the 
criminal justice system and take such measures as are necessary for the 
prevention of atrocities against women and as a result of the overall efforts of 
the Central Government most of the State and the Union Territories have set 
up special cells to deal with crime against women. Many States have set up 
police stations managed exclusively by women police personnel to deal with 
crime related to women and also inculcate a sense of confidence and security in 
women to approach police stations without fear or apprehension. 
DR.T SUBBARAMI REDDY: Mr. Chairman, when I put the question, 
what are the efforts being made to reduce these crimes against women in 2003, 
the hon. Minister has said, 'It is a State subject. However, the Government of 
India has been advising the State Governments, from time to time.' I would 
like to put a straight question to not only the Hon. Minister but also the Hon. 
Deputy Prime Minister. In New Delhi, there 
6 

[12 March, 2003] RAJYA   SABHA 
have been so many crimes taking place against women particularly, recently, 
so many college students have been harassed, and also atrocities have taken 
place against women. I would like to know what protective measures the 
Government is taking at least, in New Delhi which is under the direct control 
of the Central Government, not merely telling that it is the responsibility of 
the State Governments. That is a different issue. So, I want a reply from the 
Hon. Deputy Prime Minister. Please tell us the measures. 
SHRI I.D. SWAMI: Sir. Not only in Delhi but also throughout the 
country, various measures have already been taken to ensure that the number 
of crimes against women does not increase, rather decreases, and the women 
feel a sense of security, 
So far as Delhi is concerned, in all the districts of Delhi, there are 
separate cells for women. These women cells have been created only to 
infuse enthusiasm and confidence in the women folk so that they can 
approach those cells easily. Various other measures, sensitisation, patrolling 
and all those things, in addition, are being taken, but more important is that 
for each district in Delhi, a separate women cell has been created so far that 
purpose. 
DR. T. SUBBARAMI REDDY: Sir, my second question in this. It has 
always been found that a number of people commit crimes against women and

Commission for Women have been taken in to consideration, and the criminal

already been appointed its report is expected very soon. But whatever 
recommendations that the National Commission for women has made, those 
have been seriously followed, and necessary action is being taken. That is 
right.For trial of crimes against women,  the concept of special court is also 
being envisaged.

THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI ANANT GANGARAM GEETE): (a) 
to (c) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) and (b) According to the information received from Bharat Heavy 
Electricals Ltd., (BHEL) and Power Grid Corporation of India Limited 
(PGCIL), a prototype of "Controlled Shunt Reactor (CSR)" has been 
developed by BHEL. This CSR can be used selectively depending upon the 
system configuration and power system requirement. It aims to provide full 
reactive support to the lines during energisation and facilitate reactive power 
management in Extra High Voltage (E HV) power transmission system. The 
CSR is a significant development in the field of High Voltage Power 
Transmission as the use of this equipment is meant to improve the voltage 
profiles and reduce transmission losses. A prototype CSR of 50 MVAR  
capacity, 420 KV class developed by BHEL has been installed at 400 KV 
Itarsi sub-station of POWERGRID in September, 2001. 
(c) The requirement of CSR in the EH V system is mainly for controlling 
over-voltage where very fast control switching of reactor is desirable. 
Extensive studies are carried out to determine the size of the CSR and its 
location in the system, keeping in view its cost and requirement. Actual 
deployment of the CSR will depend on techno-economic considerations.

Demining in forward areas 
*301. SHRI K. RAHMAN KHAN: Will the Minister of DEFENCE be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that in the forward areas our forces are engaged 
in clearing mines without the aid of demining sets and mine boots; 
(b) if so, the number of Jawans killed and injured so far during the 
demining process; and 
(c) the steps proposed to be taken to stop manual demining to save 
human lives as well as complete the demining process quickly? 
THE MINISTER OF DEFENCE (SHRI GEORGE FERNANDES): (a) 
to (c) No, Sir. Demining equipment, anti-mine boots and other protective gear 
are available with our troops, who are engaged in demining operations in the 
forward areas, where land mines were laid during OPERATION 
PARAKARAM. Nevertheless, during the current demining operations, from 
October, 2002 upto 6th March, 2003, five Army personnel were killed and fifty-
nine were injured. 
Manual demining is an inescapable part of the demining process along 
with other methods, and thus cannot altogether be dispensed with. However, 
to ensure safety in demining operations, only trained army personnel who 
laid the mines and were familiar with the terrain, have been employed in 
recovery of the mines.

2230. SHRI S.S. AHLUWALIA: Will the Minister of HOME AFFAIRS 
be pleased to state:

taking action against illegal immigration from Bangladesh, Pakistan etc. 
and/or against overstay by foreign nationals; 
(b) the details of the States which are found to be failing in this regard; 
(c) whether they have explained the reasons to the Union Government 
for remaining soft on these issues inspite of its posing danger to the nation's 
security; 
(d) if so, the details thereof; and 
(e) the steps initiated by Government to enable these States to 
effectively prevent, detect and deter unauthorized presence of foreigners in the 
country? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS 
(SHRI HARIN PATHAK): (a) to (d) All State Governments are taking 
action to detect and deport illegal foreign nationals including Bangladeshis 
and Pakistanis under delegated powers of the Foreigners Act, 1946, and these 
efforts have further been intensified. 
(e) To curb illegal influx into the country, several measures have been 
taken by the Government which include strengthening of BSF and equipping 
them with modern and sophisticated equipment/gadgets, raising of additional 
battalions of BSF; reduction of gaps between border outposts, intensification of 
patrolling, accelerated programme of construction of border roads and border 
fencing, provision of surveillance equipment etc. The powers under Section 
3(2)(c) of the Foreigners Act, 1946 to detect and deport foreign nationals 
staying in India unauthorisedly have been entrusted to the State Governments 
and UT Administrations. Besides administrative instructions are also issued to them 
from time to time to launch special drives to detect foreign nationals staying 
illegally in the country for their immediate deportation.

Acceleration of reforms in mining sector 
†2242. SHRI BALKAVI BAIRAGI: Will the Minister of MINES be 
pleased to state: 
(a) steps Government are going to take to accelerate the reform process 
in the mining sector; 
(b) whether the Government have incorporated aspects like scientific 
methods related to the mining sector, protection of the environment and 
implementing the programmes related to education, creation of jobs, health 
and environmental reforms for the people living in the adjoining areas of 
mines, on priority in the said programmes of reform-process; and 
(c) if so, the details therefor? 
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
133 

RAJYA SABHA [12 March, 2003] 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF MINES (SHRI 
RAMESH BAIS): (a) to (c) Implementati on of reform process in the mining 
sector is a continuous process. The National Mineral Policy (NMP) was 
announced in 1993 and the mining sector was thrown open for private 
investment including foreign investment. To give effect to the NMP and to 
take the reforms process forward extensive changes were made in the Mines 
and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957 (MMDR Act) in 1994 
and 1999 and Rules framed thereunder were accordingly amended. 
The reform process encompassed inter alia opening up of the mining sector 
to private investment including foreign investment, delegation of powers to 
the State Governments, simplification of procedures, ushering in an investor-
friendly climate comparable with best global practices and ensuring 
systematic and scientific mining. 
Under the provision of Section 18 of the MMDR Act, 1957 Central 
Government have notified Mineral Conservation and Development Rules, 
1988 for conservation and systematic development of minerals and protection 
of environment. Appropriate penalties have been provided for contravention of 
these Rules. 
Interaction meetings with State Governments, Central Ministries/ 
Departments and the Investors in the mining sector are held from time to time 
to make the policy and procedure of grant of mineral concessions investor 
friendly and to sensitise the various stake holders about the reform process. 
Last three such meetings, a Tripartite meeting of Central Government, State 
Governments and Investors, 27th meeting of the Mineral Advisory Council 
and Conference of State Ministers of Mining and Geology have been held on 
12.11.2001, 21.9.2002 and 22.1.2003 respectively. 
In the process of ongoing consultation with the Stake-holders, it has been 
decided in the Conference of State Ministers of Mining and Geology held on 
22.1.2003 that for giving thrust to the mining sector reforms inter-alia for 
scientific methods related to mining protection of environment etc., the rules 
framed under the MMDR Act, 1957 shall incorporate provisions relating to 
minimum size of mining lease, and detailed provisions regarding mine closure 
plans and rehabilitation of mined out areas.

Adherence to safety norms 
2243. SHRI RAMACHANDRA KHUNTIA: Will the Minister of MINES 
be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware of the complete disregard for safety norms 
by the Geological Survey of India (GSI) resulting in many scientists and technical 
assistants facing life threatening diseases from radio-active chemicals they 
handle; 
(b) number of employees of CGD who died during last three years due to 
cancer and number of employees suffering from various skin diseases due to 
exposure to prolonged rediation; and

Regulatory Board norms during handling of chemicals such as cesium, Gamma 
and Nutron by the employees of Central Geophysical Division for exploration 
of minerals? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF MINES (SHRI 
RAMESH BAIS): (a) The Geological Surv ey of India (GSI) scientists and 
technical assistants always follow safety norms while handling hazardous 
radioactive chemicals and equipments which generate radiation. 
(b) No employee of GSI died or suffered from skin diseases due to 
exposure to such radiation during the last three years.

inspected the Central Geophysical Division of GSI in August, 2002 found that

aprons and radiation monitoring badges while handling chemicals and

Dabhol Power Project 
2260. SHRI S.S. AHLUWALIA: Will the Minister of POWER be 
pleased to state: 
(a) the details of investments made by Indian Financial Institutions/ 
Public Sector Banks in the Dabhol Power Corporation (DPC) both in equity of the 
company and as loan and year-wise disbursal of the same; 
(b) the present status of the DPC; 
(c) whether it has become commercially unviable project; and 
(d) if so, the measures taken and/or are contemplated to recover and secure 
the investments made by IFIs/Banks in the project? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF POWER 
(SHRIMATI JAYAWANTI MEHTA):(a) The Dabhol Power Project was 
constructed using a mix of equity and loan funds. The equity was brought in by 
the sponsors viz. Enron, General Electric, Bechtel and the Maharashtra Power 
Development Corporation Limited (MPDCL).The loan funds were advanced by 
a consortium of off-shore banks and Indian Financial Institutions/Banks 
(IFIs). The details of exposure of IFIs to Dabhol Power Company (DPC) 
(outstanding loans in respect of Phase-I and amounts disbursed plus balance to be 
disbursed in respect of Phase-ll 
163 

RAJYA SABHA [12 March, 2003] 
of the project) are indicated in Statement -I (See below). The details of year-
wise disbursement by IFIs are furnished in Statement- II (See below). The IFIs 
have not made any equity investment in the DPC. 
(b) to (d) Phase-I of the Dabhol plant (740 MW) has been shut down 
after the Maharashtra State Electricity Board (MSEB) stopped taking power 
from 29th May, 2001, following disputes with Dabhol Company ~{DPC). 
Construction work on Phase-ll (1444 MW) has also been stopped. 
The Power Purchase Agreement (PPA) in regard to the Dabhol Power Project 
was entered into between MSEB and DPC. Thus, the responsibility to restart 
Phase-I and complete Phase-ll lies with the main stakeholders viz. MSEB and 
DPC as well as the Government of Maharashtra (GoM).The IFIs led by the Industrial 
Development Bank of India (IDBI) having substantial stakes in the Dabhol Power 
Project have been trying to restructure and revive the Dabhol plant. Government 
of India has agreed to facilitate and amicable solution to the various issues in 
order to revive/restructure the project. Any scheme finalised for revival of the 
Dabhol Project would come as a comprehensive package and would have to 
resolve complex, legal, financial and technical issues. While this may take time, 
as a first step, it has been agreed that an interim revival package for restarting 
Phase-I be workded out by the concerned agencies. The National Thermal 
Power Corporation (NTPC) has agreed to act as Operation and Maintenance 
Contractor for running Phase-I. A team involving representatives from NTPC, M's GE 
India, M/s Bechtel, IDBI, MSEB and Central Electricity Authority carried out a 
preliminary inspection of the Dabhol power plant from October 28-30, 2002 to 
ascertain its condition and to work out an action plan for restart of phase-l. 
During the visit, it was found, inter-alia, that the plant and equipments had generally 
been maintained well by the firm appointed by the Court receiver for maintenance 
and preservation of the assets. However, a more detailed assessment and internal 
inspection of the equipment is felt necessary so as to ascertain the time-frame for 
restarting the plant as well as the likely expenditure involved. 
Government of Maharashtra has taken a decision to allow MSEB to draw 
power from Phase-I at an optimum level of 83% at a tariff of about Rs. 
2.80/KWH on an interim basis subject to approval of the Maharashtra Electricity 
Regulatory Commission (MERC) and High Court of Maharashtra 
164 

[12 March, 2003] RAJYA   SABHA 
which has appointed a receiver for the project, and without prejudice to 
MSEB/GoM's rights and contentions in the pending arbitration/judicial and 
MERC proceedings. In a recent communication, GoM have stressed on the need 
to restart Phase-I of the Dabhol plant at the earliest keeping in view the acute 
power crisis being faced by the State. The viability of the project will depend 
on the final restructuring of the project and related issues such as cost of fuel, 
tariff levels and off-take of power, etc.

Assistant Secretary of Energy, Ms. Vicky Bailey, in her address at an

Power Business Community about the Power Sector in India on account of 
certain contratual and payment problems being faced by the existing 
Independent Power Producers (IPPs) with US investments. She observed that it

The main issue relates to the Dobhol Power Project which is an IPP set up

these two parties to the contract as well as the Government of Maharashtra, 
who have guaranteed the payment obligations of MSEB to DPC under the 
PPA, subject to final orders on the various legal proceedings, Government of 
India has agreed to facilitate any amicable solution to the various issues so as 
to revive/restructure the Dabhol Power Project.

Covanta Asia-Pacific and El Pasco India, during a recent meeting with 
Secretary (Power) discussed their problems with the Tamil Nadu Electricity 
Board relatiny to arrears, payment of invoices and establishing of security

creation of separate Land Resource Department vetted by the Planning

Level Committee on Wastelands Development headed by Shri Mohan Dharia 
in its report submitted in December 1995, recommended the creation of a

Resources and by the Ministries of Agriculture, Environment and Forests, and 
Planning Commission with different guidelines and varying financial patterns.

Watershed Development in the Department of Land Resources and to transfer to 
it various programmes and schemes relating to the conservation, development 
and management of land resources of the country.

Fluoride affected villages in Karnataka 
2299. SHRI M.V. RAJASEKHARAN: Will the Minister of RURAL 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that high fluoride content drinking water has 
disabled villagers in many parts of the State of Karnataka; 
(b) if so, the details of persons affected due to consumption of high 
fluoride content water, district-wise in the State for the past three years; 
(c) whether Government propose to make alternative supply of drinking water 
for the villages affected by fluoride contained water; and 
(d) If so, the details of the proposals and the estimated cost thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RURAL 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRI ANNASAHEB M.K. PATIL): (a) and (b) As 
reported by the State Government, 5838 habitations in 27 districts of 
Karnataka have fluoride contamination in drinking water affecting the 
inhabitants. The survey conducted in July 2000 in Nidasoshi village and 
another survey conducted in Keerunayaka Thanda village of Gulbarga district 
in 2002 have shown 7 and 18 persons affected by skeletal fluorosis respectively. 
This disability cannot be solely attributed to fluoride content in drinking water 
alone. 
(c) and (d) Rural drinking water is a State subject. State Governments take up 
schemes/projects for providing drinking water in rural areas from their own 
resources. Government of India supplements the efforts of the State 
Governments and provides financial assistance under Accelerated Rural Water 
Supply Programme (ARWSP). Under ARWSP, upto 15% of the allotted funds 
can be utilised to tackle water quality problem which inter-alia includes 
providing safe drinking water free from fluoride contamination. 
Government of India had been sanctioning projects under Sub Mission 
Programme for providing safe drinking water free from brackishness, 
214 

[12 March, 2003] RAJYA   SABHA 
fluorides, excess iron etc. till April, 1998. Since then, powers to approve and 
implement Sub Mission projects have been delegated to the State 
Governments. State Governments have repeatedly been requested to sanction 
more and more such projects to provide safe drinking water to rural 
habitations.

[12 March, 2003] RAJYA   SABHA 
schemes/programmes sanctioned for artisans is already in place. Various schemes 
being implemented in the handicrafts sector are continuously monitored by the 
Field Offices, Regional Offices and Headquarters Office of the Development 
Commissioner (Handicarafts). 
Statement 
Schemes in operation in handloom sector 
In order to ensure sufficient availability of yarn, which is the major raw 
material in handloom sector, the Government is implementing Mill Gate Price 
Scheme under which yam is supplied by National Handloom Development 
Corporation (NHDC) to handloom weavers and organizations at mill gate 
price. Government has also issued Hank Yarn Packing Notification under 
Essential Commodities Act 1955, which obliges yarn producers who pack yarn 
for civil consumption for sale/ transfer/delivery within the country have to 
pack at least 40% of the yarn in hank form. 
Further, in order to give continued protection to the handloom weavers, 
the State Government have been instructed to arrange distribution of bank 
yarn to handloom weavers, free of excise duty (CNVAT) through designated 
organizations which could clain reimbusrsement of the incidence of 
CENVAT borne by them on such yam from the Government of India. 
In order to provide adequate and timely credit facilities at concessional rate of 
interest, refinance assistance is being provided by National Bank for 
Agriculture and Rural Development (NABARD) to State Coopertive Banks 
for financing producftion and marketing activities of Primary Weavers, 
Cooperative Societies and for procurement and marking activities of Apex 
Weavers' Cooperative Societies. 
A scheme, namely Deen Dayal Hathkargha Protsahan Yojana, was 
introduced in the year 2000-2001 to cover entire gamut of activities from basic 
input and working capital to provisions of design, marketing, publicity etc. The 
Government of India has also been providing financial assistance for development 
of exportable products and their marketing, organisation of exhibitions, fairs, 
crafts melas, setting up of urban Haats, marketing complexes, publicity and 
awareness programmes. 
227 

RAJYA SABHA [12 March, 2003] 
Apart from this, the Government has set up National Centre forTextile Design 
(NCTD) to collate and disseminate all information related to textile weaves, 
fabric, colour, design etc. to act as an electronic forum to give the weavers 
design and marketing exposure. 
The Government has also promulgated the Handloom (Reservation of 
Articles for Production), Act, 1985 under which at present 11 categories of textile 
articles are exclusively reserved for production on handlooms. 
Health Package Scheme, Workshed-cum-Housing Scheme, Thrift Fund 
Scheme, Group Insurance Scheme and a New Insurance Scheme have been in 
operation for the welfare of handloom weavers. 
Besides, 24 Weavers' Service Centres are functioning to render extension 
services, which involve transfer of design inputs, skills and technology to the 
weavers. 
Schemes in operation in handicrafts sector 
The schemes include: "Baba Saheb Ambedkar Hastshilp Vikas Yojana 
(AHVY), training and extension, design and technical upgradation, marketing 
support and services, research- and development, financial assistance to state 
handicarafts development corporations/apex societies and export promotion etc. 
"Baba Saheb Ambedkar Hastshilp Vikas Yojana" (AHVY) seeks to develop 
selected artisan clusters into professionally managed self-reliant community 
enterprises working on the priciple of effective member participation and 
mutual cooperation and aims to achieve sustainable development of the 
artisan clusters. 
Besides, 52 Handicarafts Marketing & Service Extension Centres are 
functioning all over the country to assist the artisans in the area of marketing, 
raw material, credit facilities through financial institution and design 
development etc. Further, five Regional Design & Technical Development 
Centres (RD&TDC) undertake development and dissemination of new designs 
and improvement of tools and equipment. 
The Hon'ble Prime Minister had also announced in his address to the nation 
on August 15,2002 the facility of a one time special rebate @ 10% of the value 
of the handloom products sold, so as to enable the handloom sector to dispose of 
their stock and kick-start this employment intensive industry by reviving its 
production cycle. For this, a sum of Rs. 100 crore was announced. The State 
Government have already been instructed to

Modernisation of Textiles Industry 
2315. SHRI B.J. PANDA: Will the Minister of TEXTILES be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether textile industry is modernising on massive scale to meet the 
global challenges, if so the details of such modernisation, as reported in the 
Economic Times on 17 December, 2002; 
(b) whether Government have received a good response for up-gradation 
from the Textile industry, if so, the total number of applications so far received 
and funds so far sanctioned under the Technology Upgradation Funds 
Scheme; and 
(c) incentives Government propose to extend for its growth and 
improvement of the yield to enable us to face world market? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF TEXTILES (SHRI 
BASANAGOUDA R. PATIL): (a) and (b) With a view to improve the overall 
viability of the textile and jute industries and to enable it to meet the global 
challenges, Government has launched a Technology Upgradation Fund Scheme 
(TUFS) for Textile and Jute Industries, w.e.f. 1.4.1999 for a period of 5 years, 
i.e. upto 31 st March 2004. The main feature of the scheme js that it provides a 
reimbursement of 5% point on the interest charged by the lending agency on a 
project of technology upgradation in conformity with this scheme.There is no cap 
on funding under this scheme. With effect from 1st Jan., 2002, an option has 
been provided to the Small Scale Textile and Jute Industries to avail of either 12 
percent Credit Linked Capital Subsidy (CLCS-TUFS) or 5 percent interest 
reimbursement under TUFS. 
232 

[12 March, 2003] RAJYA   SABHA 
As on December 31,2002, under the TUFS, 2023 applications have been 
received with a project cost of Rs. 15810 crore and a loan requirement of Rs. 9095 
crore. 1782 applications have been sanctioned for a loan amount of Rs. 6101 
crore. Rs. 4203 crore have been disbursed in respect of 1430 applications. 
(c) The Government has provided a number of incentives for the growth 
of textile sector and improvement of yield, which include:— 
i) Technology Mission on Cotton 
Government has launched the Technology Mission on Cotton during 1999-
2000 for a period of 5 years. This Mission has four Mini Missions to bring 
about all around improvement in the production, productivity and quality of 
cotton through research, transfer of technology and improvement in the raw 
cotton processing and marketing. 
ii) Textile Package in the Budget 2003-04 
In the current budget of 2003-04, to strengthen the textile industry, 
Central Value Added Tax (CENVAT) chain has been completed and the 
number of exemptions and deemed credit schemes have been withdrawn. 
The excise duty on fibres, yarn, fabrics/made ups and readymade garments 
(RMG) has been reduced considerably. 
iil) Reduction in Customs duty on Textile machinery 
In order to facilitate import of textile machinery with state of the art 
technology, list of 175 items of specified textile machinery attract 
concessional rate of import duty. In the current budget basic import duty on 
additional 39 numbers of textile machinery has been reduced to 5%. 
iv) De-reservation of Garment Industry and raising of Small Scale 
Industry (SSI) limit 
Garment industry has been de-reserved from SSI sector with effect from 
1st January, 2001 to encourage large-scale investments in the garment sector 
and achieving of economies of scale. Small-scale investment limit has been 
raised to Rs. 5 Crores in case of knitting and knitwear items. 
v) Integrated Apparel Park Scheme 
Governmet has formulated "Apparel Parks for Exports" with a view to 
involve State Government in promoting investment in the apparel sector. The 
Central Government will give as a grant 75% or maximum of Rs. 10 crore of the 
capital expenditure incurred by the State Government on the 
233 

RAJYA SABHA [12 March, 2003] 
infrastructure facilities of the Apparel Park, while the remaining 25% will be 
born by the agency. This grant shall be limited to a maximum of Rs. 10 crores. 
vi)Textile Centres Infrastructure Development Scheme (TCIDS) 
Government has launched Textile Centres Infrastructure Development 
Scheme (TCIDS)" for plugging critical infrastrcture gaps in traditional 
textile/apparel clusters to help the units located therein to become globally 
competitive. 
The central assistance under the scheme is available to the extent of 100% of 
the critical components of the project in respect of Common Effluent Plant, 
improving water supply and drainage facilities and construction of creche 
building for apparel units, whereas the other components would be funded on 
75:25 between Centre and State/reputed agencies concerned.

includes, modernisation, payment of statutory dues, secured loans, VRS to

would be given attractive VRS package. The remaining workers will continue 
in their jobs.

STATEMENT BY THE PRIME MINISTER REGARDING IRAQ SITUATION 
THE PRIME MINISTER (SHRI ATAL BIHARI VAJPAYEE) : Mr. 
Chairman, Sir, the situation relating to Iraq has been rapidly evolving over the 
past few weeks. India has consistently stood for a peaceful resolution of the 
Iraq issue. The peace and prosperity of the Gulf is of vital interest to India 
given our long standing political, cultural and economic ties with the countries 
of the region. There are over 3.5 million Indians working in the Gulf, whose 
welfare is of great concern to us. Their remittances are an important source of 
foreign exchange for the country. Over 60 per cent of India's crude oil imports 
are sourced from the region. The Gulf countries have also emerged as 
important destinations for our exports. 
India recognizes the validity of the unanimous decision of the UN 
Security Council in its Resolution 1441, which provides for the disarmament of 
Iraq and also reaffirms the sovereignty and territorial integrity of Iraq, Kuwait 
and the neighbouring States. Resolution 1441 provides a stringent regime of 
inspections designed to meet the international community's desire that 
Weapons of Mass Destruction are eliminated from Iraq. We believe that Iraq 
must cooperate actively with the inspection process and comply fully with all 
relevant Security Council Resolutions. If the pace of this cooperation had 
been quicker, it may have enabled United Nations Monitoring Verification and 
Inspection Commission and the International Atomic Energy Agency to certify 
to the UN Security Council that Iraq was in full compliance of Resolution 1441. 
The work of the inspectors is continuing in Iraq. The Security Council 
should decide on what further action needs to be taken. The international 
community must take a very careful look both at the objective of achieving 
Iraq's full compliance with UN resolutions and at the means to be adopted to 
reach this goal. This can best be achieved by a collective decision through the 
United Nations. If permitting more time and formulation of clearer criteria can 
facilitate a decision within the UN framework, we believe this option should be 
given a chance. We hope that the members of the Security Council will 
harmonise their positions to ensure that its final decision enhances the 
legitimacy and credibility of the United Nations. If unilateralism prevails, the 
U.N. would be deeply scarred, with disastrous consequences for the world 
order. The Government of India would strongly urge that no military action be 
taken, which does not have the collective concurrence of the international 
community. 
249 

RAJYA SABHA [12 March, 2003] 
India has voiced its concern on various occasions about the difficult 
humanitarian situation in Iraq. The Iraqi people have suffered severe 
shortages and hardships for over a decade. We have consistently stated that 
if Iraq complies fully with the provisions of relevant Security Council 
resolutions, then sanctions against that country should be lifted. 
While we sincerely hope, in the interest of all humanity, that the 
matter can be resolved peacefully through the United Nations, my Government 
has drawn up contingency plans to deal with any eventuality. There are less 
than 50 Indian nationals in Iraq at present and they have all been advised to 
leave the country in the coming days. It is unlikely that there would be any 
large scale dislocation of the Indian communities in the neighbouring countries 
on a possible outbreak of hostilities. Nevertheless the Ministry of Civil Aviation 
has drawn up plans to evacuate Indians, if necessary. The Ministry of 
Petroleum and Natural Gas has taken steps to shore up our inventories of 
crude oil. While no major dislocation in crude oil imports is envisaged, India 
has adequate foreign exchange reserves to meet a higher crude oil import bill 
if prices continue to rise in the short run. Thank you.

Mr. Chairman: Question No. 326. 
Boundary Dispute with Myanmar 
*326. SHRI RISHANG KEISHING: Will the Minister of EXTERNAL 
AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a)whether any boundary dispute exists between Myanmar and India; 
(b) if so, what efforts have been made to settle the dispute in a friendly 
and peaceful way; and 
(c) the steps taken to further improve and strengthen the friendly 
relations between the two countries? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF EXTERNAL 
AFFAIRS (SHRI VINOD KHANNA): (a) to (c) Sir, a Statement is placed on 
the Table of the House. 
Statement 
Boundary dispute with Myanmar 
1. Under the boundary agreement of 1967, a Joint Boundary 
Commission was constituted for demarcating the India-Myanmar boundary. 
Out of 1643 kms. of the India-Myanmar boundary, demarcation of 1472 kms. has 
been completed. 136 kms. in the Lohit sub-sector of Arunachal Pradesh and 
35 kms. in the Kabaw valley of Manipur sector remains undemarcated. 
Although the undemarcated sectors are not an issue in bilateral relations, 
discussions in this regard are held in the institutional mechanisms for 
boundary-related issues. 
2. It was also agreed in the Joint Boundary Commission by the two 
Governments to maintain all boundary pillars and to move forward with joint 
inspection, repair and restoration of pillars. The first meeting between the Heads 
of Survey Deparments of India an d Myanmar was held in Yangon in 
September 1993. 
21 

RAJYA SABHA [13 March, 2003] 
3. At the meeting of Heads of Survey Departments held in New Delhi in 
October 2002, the work plan for the field seasons 2002-2003 and 2003-2004 
was finalised. A Director level meeting of the Survey Departments was held 
at Tamu-Moreh in December 2002.The work on joint inspection has 
progressed smoothly. 
4. Our relations with Myan mar reflect our common desire to cooperate 
with each other to promote peace and tranquillity along the border, achieve 
sustained economic development in both our countries and to foster people-
to-people interaction. To this end, our effort has been to strengthen the 
friendly relations through high-level dialogue and increased economic 
interaction through collaborative projects. There are institutional mechanisms 
for maintaining regular dialogue on issues of mutual concern which meet 
from time to time. 
SHRI RISHANG KEISHING: Mr. Chairman, Sir, according to the 
statement, 136 Kms. in the Lohit sector of Arunachal Pradesh and 35 Kms. in 
the Kabaw valley of Manipur sector remain undemarcated. I would like to 
know how this happened. Was it that this area was never demarcated? Or, 
though the demarcation was done, the boundary stones or boundary pillars, 
etc. were damaged, or, removed? How soon will this be demarcated? 
SHRI VINOD KHANNA: Sir, a boundary agreement was signed 
between India and Myanmar in March, 1967. Under this agreement, a Joint 
Boundary Commission, composed of officials representing the two countries 
was constituted and charged with the task of planning and carrying out 
demarcation of the Indo-Myanmar boundary. 
Sir, the hon. Member is talking about 136 Kms. in the Lohit sub-sector of 
Arunachal Pradesh and 36 Kms. in  Kabaw valley sector of Manipur. The 
demarcation in the Lohit Sector has not been undertaken due to the reluctance 
of Myanmar to associate itself with the Sino Indian border, which has been 
mentioned in the statement. The demarcation of the boundary in Arunachal 
sector has not been discussed after March, 1976. This is because the boundary 
begins from the trijunction of India, China and Myanmar; and Myanmar 
desires to have a tripartite meeting organisation.

*330. SHRI C. P. THIRUNAVUKKARASU: Will the Minister of 
COMMUNICATIONS AND INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether Government propose to amend the Indian Post Office Act, 
1898 to open postal sector to private operators; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether it is a fact that the western countries have not opened up their 
own postal services; and 
(d) if so, the reason for privatisation of the postal services? 
THE MINISTER OF COMMUNICATIONS AND INFORMATION 
TECHNOLOGY (SHRI ARUN SHOURIE): (a) to (d) A Statement is laid on 
the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) and (b) Indian Post Office (Amendment) Bill, 2002 has been 
introduced in the Lok Sabha on 17.5.2002 to bring about qualitative 
improvement in the services with more customer friendly features. Under the 
Indian Post Office Act, 1898 exclusive privilege of conveying letters only is 
reserved to the Government. This privilege is sought to be retained with the 
Department in the Indian Post Office (Amendment) Bill, 2002. 
(c) No, Sir. Some western countries have opened the postal sector while 
reserving their exclusive privilege in respect of certain products and services. 
The position varies from country to country. 
(d) There is no proposal as yet to privatise postal services. 
'SHRI C. P. THIRUNAVUKKARASU: Mr. Chairman, Sir, my question 
was: Are you going to privatise the postal service? The reply should have 
been that there is no proposal to privatise the postal service, or,

mentioned, there is no proposal as yet to privatise the postal service.' 
Already, an amendment of section 4 of the Act has been sought. Section 4(a) 
of the Postal Service Act stipulates the conditions for introducing courier 
services. So, it paves the way for privatisation. 
SHRI ARUN SHOURIE: Sir, there is complete confusion. There is no 
proposal at all, at the moment, to privatise any of the post offices. The 
question, as we understood it, was about this sector as a whole. In many 
cases, sectors are opened up. The banking sector has been opened up, but no 
nationalised bank has been privatised. Similarly, with the introduction of 
courier services, the first element of transmitting parcels etc. by private sector 
is coming. It is only with reference to that. As far as the rest of the Postal 
Service Departments are concerned, they continue as they are. 
Sir, the question is, actually, about amendment of the Indian Post Office 
Act, not privatisation, On this, the amendment of section 4 is only to enable—
because as of now there are only about 2,300 courier companies in India, they 
are completely unregulated—many things, which even agencies of 
Government for intelligence purposes or for the purpose of prevention of 
crime require, but can't be extended to them because of the 1898 Act. For that 
reason, amendment of section 4 was among the amendments suggested, and it 
is before the Standing Committee. When the Standing Committee comes back 
to us, we will inform the House.

Transfer of industries to private hands due to disinvestment policy 
*340. SHRI LALU PRASAD: Will the Minister of DISINVESTMENT 
be pleased to state: 
43 

RAJYA SABHA [13 March, 2003] 
(a) whether Government's existing policy of disinvestment has led to 
transfer of several important industries to private hands; 
(b) whether this transfer would lead to gradual reduction in the number 
of employees working in these units; and 
(c) whether Government propose to tackle this issue; if so, by when and 
in what manner? 
THE MINISTER OF DISINVESTMENT (SHRI ARUN SHOURIE): (a) 
During the period 1999 to 2002, the Government has transferred management 
control through strategic sale in Modem Food Industries (India) Ltd. (MFIL), 
Lagan Jute Machinery Company (LJMC), Paradeep Phosphates Ltd. (PPL), 
Bharat Aluminium Co. Ltd. (BALCO), Maruti Udyog Ltd. (MUL), HTL 
Ltd., CMC Ltd., IBP Ltd., Videsh Sanchar Nigam Ltd. (VSNL), Hindustan 
Zinc Ltd. (HZL), and Indian Petrochemicals Corpn. Ltd. (IPCL) and 100% 
Government share in 19 hotel properties and one hotel (through lease-cum-
management) of India Tourism Development Corpn. Ltd. (ITDC) and 3 
hotels of Hotel Corporation of India. 
(b) Transfer of management control to a strategic partner cannot be 
linked directly to employment. In the case of CMC Ltd., there has been a 
net addition in employment of 425 against the employees strength of 
3119 at the time of disinvestment. The data compiled for nine disinvested 
companies including CMC Ltd., ten hotels of ITDC and one hotel of Hotel 
Corporation India shows that against an initial employment level of 43,171 
at the time of disinvestment there was a total attrition of 3,733 employees, 
while 964 employees have been recruited. Therefore, the net loss in 
employment was 2,769, which is around 6% of employment at the time 
of disinvestment, of which 663 were on account of retirement and 
resignation. There have been no cases of retrenchment post disinvestment. 
Out of the net loss of employment of 2769, over three fourth, or 2145 
jobs are accounted for by just two companies; MFIL, BALCO. However, 
in the case of these two companies, 3401 jobs were lost in the period 
1991 -92 till date of disinvestment, indicating that the loss of employment 
is not linked to disinvestment alone, but relates to the restructuring 
requirements of these companies. 
(c) Protection of employees' interest is an integral part of the 
disinvestment policy. Adequate provisions are made in the Transactions 
Agreements, executed as a part of strategic sale, to ensure that there is 
44 

[13 March, 2003] RAJYA   SABHA 
no retrenchment of employees for one year after disinvestment and even 
thereafter separation is possible only under the Voluntary Retirement Scheme 
as applicable under Department of Public Enterprises guidelines or the 
Voluntary Retirement Scheme which was prevailing in the company prior to 
disinvestment whichever is more beneficial for the employees. Productive 
use of the existing assets of the disinvested PSUs and the creation of new 
assets make the enterprises more competitive and thereby provide the best 
guarantee of continued employment; that also is one sustainable way of 
ensuring expansion of employment.

2320. SHRI P. PRABHAKAR REDDY: Will the PRIME MINISTER be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have decided to install country's first 
plutonium-based commercial fast breeder reactor in the Indira Gandhi Centre

generation of additional energy resources and if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE DEPARTMENT OF ATOMIC 
ENERGY (SHRI SATYABRATA MOOKHERJEE): (a) Yes, Sir. A proposal 
for administrative approval and project financial sanction for setting up of a 
500 MWe Prototype Fast Breeder Reactor (PFBR) at Kalpakkam, Tamil 
Nadu is under process with the Government of India. 
(b) and (c) A three stage Nuclear Power Programme has been envisaged 
by the Department of Atomic Energy, right from its inception. With the 
construction of Pressurised Heavy Water Reactors (PHWR), the first stage of 
the Indian nuclear power programme has attained a level of maturity. At 
present, the Department proposes to launch the second stage of setting up of 
Fast Breeder Reactors (FBR) for power generation. This stage is based on 
Plutonium fuelled reactors with depleted uranium as the blanket. The PFBR 
will add 500 MWe of nuclear power generation capacity to the Southern 
Grid.

revised pulse duration announced by Telecom Regulatory Authority of India

tariffs for all Telecom Services, accordingly TRAI has issued the

are in form of the Standard Tariff Package and the operators including 
Government sector operators are at liberty to offer tariff packages with

automatic route.

Statement 
FDI policy in Telecom Sector Present FDI 
Policy for the Telecom sector is as under:— 
1. In Basic, Cellular Mobile, National Long Distance, International 
Long Distrance, Value Added service and Global Mobile 
Personal Communications by Satellite, FDI is limited to 49% 
(under automatic route) subject to grant of license from 
Department of Telecommunications and adherence by the 
companies (who are investing and the companies in which 
investment is being made) to the license conditions for foreign 
equity cap and lock-in period for transfer and addition of equity 
and other license provisions. 
2. Foreign direct investment upto 74% permitted, subject to 
licensing and security requirements for the following:— 
88 

[13 March, 2003] RAJYA   SABHA 
(i) Internet Service (with gateways) 
 (ii) Infastructure Providers (category-ll) 
 (iii) Radio Paging Service 
3. FDI upto 100% permitted in respect of the following telecom 
services:— 
(i) ISPs not providing gateways (both for satellite and submarine 
cables); 
(ii) Infastructure Providers providing dark fibre (IP Category I); 
(iii) Electronic Mail; and 
(iv) Voice Mail 
The above would be subject to following conditions:— 
(i) FDI upto 100% is allowed subject to the conditions that such 
companies would divest 26% of their equity in favour of Indian 
public in 5 years, if these companies are listed in other parts of 
the world. 
(ii) The above services would be subject to licensing and security 
requirements, wherever required. 
(iii) Proposals for FDI beyond 49% shall be considered by FIPB on 
case to case basis. 
4. In manufacturing sector 100% FDI is permitted under automatic 
route. 
5. Foreign Direct Investment upto 49% is also permitted in an 
investment company, set up for making investment in the telecom companies 
licensed to operate telecom services. Investment by these investment 
companies in a telecom service company is treated as part of domestic equity 
and is not set off against the foreign equity cap. 
6. Non-convertible preference share does not attract sectoral cap.

Economic cost of FCI on wheat and rice 
2374. DR. DASARINARAYANA RAO: Will the Minister of 
CONSUMER AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION be pleased 
to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the Administrative Staff College of India, 
Hyderabad had recently submitted its report on ways and means to reduce 
economic cost of FCI on wheat and rice; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) what action Government have taken thereon? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF CONSUMER 
AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION (SHRI SUBASH 
MAHARIA):(a)Yes, Sir. 
(b)The main findings and recommendations made in the Study Report of 
the Administrative Staff College of India, Hyderabad are given in the 
statement (See below). 
(c) The recommendations made in the report are under examination. 
105 

RAJYA SABHA [13 March, 2003] 
Statement 
The main findings and recommendations made in the Study Report of 
the Administrative Staff College of India, Hyderabad to suggest ways and 
meaqs to cut down the administrative and economic cost of the Food 
Corporation of India are as under:— 
1. FCI should be more cost conscious and prepare a cost budget for its 
operations. 
2. FCI should take up measures for cost control and examine issues 
related to direct purchase of grains from the farmers which will save 
the payment of commission to the Arthiyas, use of cheaper HDPE/PP 
bags instead of gunnies, reduction in storage cost by reducing 
departmental labour and reverting to contract labour, reduction in 
transport costs by rationalizing road transport contracts, reduction in 
transit losses by introduction of a system of weighment of railway 
rakes, reduction in buffer carrying costs by permitting disposal of 
excess holding through market sales etc. 
3. For making the FCI viable, the Government of India should give up 
control over any two of the three factors consisting of (i) fixation of 
procurement price; (ii) fixing of procurement quantity; and (iii) fixing 
of issue price. 
4. The FCI should immediately implement a computerized Management 
Information System. 
5. The system of physical verification of stocks by internal controls and 
outside agencies should be augmented. 
6. the Railways should taken full responsibility of the consignments 
received for transport. They should not only issue a clear RR, but 
deliver the consignment in the same condition at the destination to the 
FCI, fulfilling the obligation of the Bailee under the Contract Act. 
7. Financing of buffer stocks with borrowed funds from the Banking 
Sector should be done away with and the same should be financed 
through Government grant/equity. 
8. Decentralized procurement should be encouraged. 
106 

[13 March, 2003] RAJYA   SABHA 
9. The FCI may sell out all storage assets to the Central Warehousing 
Corporation which can become a prominent storage agency in the 
country. 
10. The FCI should be given greater autonomy to carry out its operaitons. 
11. The study has also recommended the "unbundling" of FCI operations 
either functionally or spatially. This could be achieved either by 
dividing FCI operations by handing over procurement to State 
Governments, distribution to the railways and physical verification 
and storage to CWG. An alternative would be to create State FCIs 
which will carry out ail operations within the State. The Union FCI 
will only procure, hold and allocate buffer-stocks.

Musharraf's Assurance to end cross Border Terrorism 
2409. SHRI RAJ KUMAR DHOOT: Will the Minister of EXTERNAL 
AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Pakistan President Pervez Musharraf in his 
speech on the 12th January, 2002 committed to end Pakistan's practice of 
supporting cross border terrorism in Jammu and Kashmir; 
(b) if so, what has been Government's experience in this regard; and 
(c) what diplomatic efforts have been made to ensure that Pakistan 
fulfills its commitments? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF EXTERNAL 
AFFAIRS (SHRI VINOD KHANNA): (a) On 12th January, 2002 Pakistan 
President General Pervez Musharraf declared that Pakistan would no longer 
allow its territory to be used for any terrorist activity anywhere in the world 
and that no organisation in Pakistan would be allowed to indulge in terrorism 
in the name of Kashmir. Subsequently, on May 27 and June 6,2002 General 
Musharfaf committed to end cross border infiltration on a permanent basis. 
142 

[13 March, 2003] RAJYA   SABHA 
(b) Pakistan took some limited, action against some terrorist groups and 
arrested some iow-levei cadres. However, there was no subsequent follow up 
action and most of them were soon released. Leaders of banned terrorist 
organizations, Hafiz Saeed and Masood Azhar, were also released and 
allowed to carry on their activities. Alter initial phases of decline in 
infiltration after the January 12, 2002 and May 27, 2002 speeches, infiltration 
reached its earlier levels in September 2002 and continues even today on a 
significant scale. There is no evidence of any significant attempts made by 
Pakistan to dismantle the infrastructure that supports and feeds cross border 
infiltration and terrorism including launching stations, communication 
centres, training camps and funding. 
(c) Government has taken number of steps considered appropriate and 
effective and has been bringing to the attention of the international 
community facts pertaining to Pakistan's sponsorship of cross border 
infiltration and terrorism. As a result  of India's efforts, it is widely 
acknowledged that Pakistan has not lived up to the promises maae by 
President Musharraf in his 12th January and 27th May, 2002 speeches and 
there is recognition of Pakistan being an epicentre of international terrorism. 
Many countries have called upon Pakistan to fulfil its commitment to end 
cross border infiltration and terrorism, to dismantle the infrastructure of 
support to terrorism and stop Pakistan from continuing to serve as a platform 
for international terrorism.

discussions with the Hon'ble Prime Minister of India. Mr. Miller also called 
on the Hon'ble President of India and met the Deputy Prime Minister, the 
Minister of External Affairs, Raksha Mantriand the Leader of Opposition in 
the Lok Sabha.These discussions covered the entire range of bilateral 
relations and important regional and international issues of mutual interest. 
During his visit to Bangalore, the Prime Minister of Poland also met the

technological establishments there. An agreement on Cooperation in 
Combating Organised Crime and International Terrorism, as well as an 
Agreement on Cooperation in Defence and an Extradition Treaty were

Poland's views on combating terrorism were similar to those of India. The 
Agreement on Cooperation in Combating Organised crime and International 
Terrorism aims at enhancing the cooperation of the two countries in this 
sphere by providing for exchange of documentation, information and 
experience on the activities of persons indulging inorganized crime and 
terrorism, especially those engaging in illegal production, distribution, and 
trade in narcotic and psychotropic substances, trafficking in persons and illicit 
trade in arms; thefts of radioactive and nuclear substances as well as their 
illegal trade; counterfeiting and forgeries of money; money laundering, as 
well as the offences relating to funding of international terrorism. The 
Agreement also provides for extending operational co-operation between 
respective authorities of the two countries. The Extradition Treaty will 
facilitate extradition of any person who is wanted for prosecuton for, or is 
convicted of an extraditable offence committed within the territory of the 
Requesting State, and is found within the territory of the Requested State.

Fixation of Minimum Wages 
2418. SHRI MANOJ BHATTACHARYA: Will the Minister of 
LABOUR be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have taken any final decision with regard to the 
fixation of minimum wages; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether the decision has been taken in consultation with various

(e) if answer to part (a) above is in the negative, the reasons therefor; 
and 
148 

[13 March, 2003] RAJYA   SABHA 
(f) by when a decision thereon is likely to be finalised? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF LABOUR (SHRI 
VIJAY GOEL): (a) to (f) The minimum wages are already being fixed under 
the Minimum Wages Act, 1948 primarily with a view to safeguard the 
interest of unorganised sector workers who are generally illiterate and 
vulnerable to exploitation due to lack of bargaining power. Under the 
provisions of the Act, both Central and State Governments are the 
appropriate Governments to fix minimum wages in respect of scheduled 
employments under their respective jurisdictions. There are 45 scheduled 
employments in Central sphere and 1232 in the State spheres. In fixing the 
minimum wages, the norms recommended by the Indian Labour Conference 
(ILC) in its 15th Session and subsequent judicial pronouncements are taken 
into account. The ILC comprises representatives of Central Trade Union 
Organisations, State Governments and Employers' Associations. The 
Government is exploring the possibilities of enactment of a unified Law on 
Wages including minimum wages in the light of the recommendations of the 
Second National Commission on Labour. However, given the procedures 
involved, it may not be possible to specify any time frame for the same. 
Elimination of Child Labour 
2419. SHRI SURENDRA LATH: Will the Minister of LABOUR be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether any steps are being taken by Government to eliminate child 
labour and bonded labour in the country; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) where there are still child labour and bonded labour in some parts of 
the country; 
(d) if so, the steps taken to identify and rehabilitate them? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF LABOUR (SHRI 
VIJAY GOEL): (a) and (b) In order to eliminate child labour in the country, 
the Government had adopted a National Child Labour Policy in 1987. This 
policy consists of three components: 
(i) A Legislative Action Plan; 
149 

RAJYA SABHA [13 March, 2003] 
(ii) Focussing of general development programmes for benefiting child 
labour wherever possible; and 
(iii) Project based plan of action for launching of projects for the welfare of 
working children in areas of high concentration of child labour. 
The Central Government has enacted the Bonded Labour System 
(Abolition) Act, 1976, which provides for identification, release and 
rehabilitation of bonded labourers. The Act provides for setting up of 
Vigilance Committees at District and Sub-Divisional levels to monitor and 
review the incidence of bonded labour on a regular basis. 
(c) Yes, Sir. 
(d) The Government of India has been implementing two schemes for 
rehabilitation of children withdrawn from work, namely the scheme of 
National Child Labour Projects (NCLP) and the scheme of Grant-in-aid to 
Voluntary Organisations. The major activity under the NCLP is running 
special schools/centres for rehabilitation of children withdrawn from work 
through non-formal/formal education, vocational training, nutrition, health 
care, stipend etc. So far, 100 NCLPs have been sanctioned for coverage of 
2.11 lakh children in 13 child labour endemic states. 
A Centrally Sponsored Plan Scheme for rehabilitation of bonded 
labourers has been in operation since May, 1978. Under the scheme, 
rehabilitation grant to the extent of Rs. 10,000/- per freed bonded labour was 
provided upto March, 2000 for rehabilitation of bonded labour. The scheme 
has been revised since May, 2000 and rehabiliation grant has been raised to 
Rs. 20,000/- per freed bonded labour. The expenditure is shared equally by 
the Central and State Government concerned on 50:50 basis except in the 
case of the seven North-Eastern States where such assistance is given on 
100% subsidy basis. In the revised scheme, provision has been made for 
giving 100% grant of Rs. 2.00 lakh to State Government for conducting 
survey on bonded labourers in a district once in three years, Rs. 10.00 lakh 
per annum to a State for awareness generation and Rs. 5.00 lakh per annum to 
State for evaluatory study etc.

Conference on unorganised labour 
2423. SHRI S. M. LAL JAN BASHA: Will the Minister of LABOUR be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that National Labour Institute organised a 
conference on unorganised labour, recently; 
. (b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) the conclusion arrived thereat; and 
(d) the steps proposed by the National Labour Institute to keep in touch 
with NGOs to improve the conditions of the unorganised labour? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF LABOUR (SHRI 
VIJAY GOEL): (a) to (d) Yes, Sir. A two-day National Seminar on 
'Unorganised Sector Labour: social protection, skill development and 
166 

[13 March, 2003) RAJYA   SABHA 
legislative intervention on unorganised labour was organized on 7-8 
November, 2002 by V.V. Giri National Labour Institute, which was attended 
by the representatives of trade unions, employees, State Governments and 
Central Ministries, NGOs and other social partners. The focus of the Seminar

Minimum wages 
† 2424. SHRI BASHISTHA NARAIN SINGH: Will the Minister of 
LABOUR be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the provision of the minimum wages for men, women and 
minor labourers has been made under the Minimum Wages Act; 
(b) if so, the reasons for the disparity in the wages in the States; and 
(c) the steps being taken by Government to remove the disparity and to 
bring uniformity in the interest of the labourers? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF LABOUR (SHRI 
VIJAY GOEL): (a) to (c)The Minimum Wages Act, 1948 does not 
discriminate between men and women in so far as fixation or revision of 
minimum wages are concerned. Women workers get the same wages as the 
men do. However different rates of minimum wages are fixed for children 
and adolescent labourer. 
There is disparity in the minimum wages throughout the country due to 
variations in socio-economic and agro-climatic conditions, cost of living, 
productivity, paying capacity, local conditions etc. 
† Original notice of the question was received in Hindi.  
167 

RAJYA SABHA [13 March, 2003] 
With a view to reduce disparity, the Central Government issued 
guide'ines in 1987 for setting up Regional Minimum Wages Advisory 
Committees. These Committees have made a number of recommendations 
which include reduction in disparity in minimum wages of different states 
within a region, setting up inter-state Coordination Council, consultation with 
neighbouring States while fixing/ revising minimum wages etc. The Central 
Government also suggested to the State Governments in Februrary, 1999 for 
constitution of Committees of Officials from adjoining States in order to 
explore uniformity in minimum wages in the States within a region. The 
Central Government has mooted the concept of National Floor Level Wage 
also and has been requesting the State Governments to ensure that in none of 
the scheduled employments the minimum wage is below the national floor 
level wage. The floor level wage was fixed initially at Rs. 35/- in 1996. 
Thereafter it has been revised from time to time, the last revision being made 
to Rs. 50/-per day w.e.f. 1.9.2002. 
Plan to check migration from villages 
† 2425. PROF. M. M. AGARWAL: Will the Minister of LABOUR be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have formulated any national plan to check 
migration of people from villages to cities; 
(b) whether Government have formulated any effective policy to reduce 
the increasing rate of unemployment in the villages; 
(c) if so, whether Government have made any assessment of the 
increasing number of unemployed persons in the villages; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF LABOUR (SHRI 
VIJAY GOEL): (a) The Government has no specific plan to check the 
migration of people from villages to cities. 
(b) The Special Group headed by Dr. S. P. Gupta, Member, Planning 
Commission was constituted to suggest strategy and programme for creation 
of one crore employment opportunities per year during each year of the 10th 
Plan period. The Group proposed creation of 5 crore 
† Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
168 

[13 March, 2003] RAJYA   SABHA 
opportunities over the 10th Plan period. Out of these, nearly 2 crore have to 
come from specific employment generation programmes and 3 crore from 
growth buoyancy. The special employment generation programme will be 
implemented in the rural area also. 
Government is also implementing special programmes for eradication of 
poverty and generation of employment in the rural areas. These include 
Swama Jayanti Gram Swarozgar Yojana (SJGSY), Jawahar Gram Smriddhi 
Yojana (JGSY), Employment Assurance Scheme (EAS), Pradhan Mantri 
Gram Sadak Yojana (PMGSY) and Food for work programme. These 
schemes/programmes are expected to reduce the incidence of 
unemployment/underemployment in rural areas as also to check migration of 
people from villages to cities. 
(c) and (d) As per the estimates available from labour force surveys of 
National Sample Survey Organisation estimated number of unemployed 
persons in rural areas has gone up from approximately 3.35 million in 1993-
94 to 4.38 million in 1999-2000. 
Impact of liberalisation 
† 2426. SHRI KRIPAL PARMAR: Will the Minister of LABOUR be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that consequent upon new economic policy, near 
about one lac factories have been closed down throughout the country and 
almost one crore labourers have lost their jobs; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) the steps taken in the interest of the labourers in this age of economic 
liberalisation; and 
(d) whether labour laws providing justice to the labourers would be 
made more effective, if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF LABOUR (SHRI 
VIJAY GOEL): (a) and (b) According to information provided by Labour 
Bureau, 2165 industrial units have closed down and approximately 1.57 lakh 
workers have been affected since 1992. 
(c) and (d) Safeguards are provided under various labour legislations

to protect the interests of the workers. However, review and updation of these 
laws is a continuous process. Amendments in the Trade Unions Act, 1926 
and the Workmen's Compensation Act, 1923 have been carried out recently. 
Besides this, a scheme for counselling, re-training and re-deployment of 
rationalized workers of Central Public Sector Undertakings has also been 
introduced from 2001 -2002 with a thrust on self-employment of the 
rationalized employees.

be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that growth of employment in organised industry 
and services both in the public and the private sector has lagged far behind 
the overall growth of the economy;

[13 March, 2003] RAJYA   SABHA 
(b) if so, the details thereof and the reasons therefor; and 
(c) the steps proposed to boost up the employment opportunities in 
various sectors? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF LABOUR (SHRI 
VIJAY GOEL): (a) and (b) As per the information available from 
Employment Market Information Programme of Directorate General of 
Employment & Training, employment in the organised sector during 2000-
2001 declined by approximately 0.61% as against 0.98% per annum growth

(c) The Tenth Plan document focusses on providing gainful high quality

attention would be paid to the policy environment influencing a wide range

2460. SHRI DINA NATH MISHRA: Will the Minister of SMALL 
SCALE INDUSTRIES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that credit flow to Small Scale Industries sector as 
percentage of net bank credit and also as percentage of priority sector net 
bank credit is decreasing since last few years; 
(b) whether it is also a fact that the Planning Commission and the 
Reserve Bank of India have shown concern over shrinking of credit to SSIs; 
and 
(c) if so, what are Government's plan to arrest this falling credit trend 
and re-orient the focus of lending institutions towards granting increased 
credit to Small Scale Industries? 
THE MINISTER OF SMALL SCA LE INDUSTRIES (DR. C.P. 
THAKUR): (a) to (c) As per the information received from the Reserve Bank 
of India (RBI), the percentage of SSI advances to Net Bank Credit (NBC) as 
also to that of priority sector advances of Public Sector Banks shows a 
declining trend over the last few years. Considering the concerns regarding 
this declining trend, the Planning Commission convened a meeting on 10th 
December, 2002 under the Chairmanship of the Deputy Chairman to discuss 
various issues relating credit flow to SSI sector. As a follow up, the meeting 
of the Reserve Bank of India (RBI)'s Standing Advisory Committee on Flow 
of Institutional Credit to SSI sector was held on 15th January, 2003. Based on 
the decisions taken in this meeting, the RBI has advised the banks inter-alia 
to consider budgeting their growth in advances to SSI sector keeping in view 
the trends in growth of net bank credit less food credit. Further, as per the 
Union Budget 2003-04, the Indian Banks' Association is advising all its 
member banks to adopt an interest rate band of 2 per cent above and below 
Prime Lending Rate (PLR) as announced by the State Bank of India.

2466. SHRIMATI S.G. INDIRA: Will the Minister of SMALL SCALE

from developed countries; 
(b) if so.the reasons therefor; and

such imports? 
THE MINISTER OF SMALL SCALE INDUSTRIES (DR. C.P. 
THAKUR): (a) and (b) As  per the international commitments, India has 
removed Quantitative Restrictions (QRs), which were being maintained 
earlier on balance of payment grounds on different items including items 
reserved for small scale sector. 
(c) Government is constantly monitoring the impact of the removal of 
QRs and WTO Agreements on the economy including the Small Scale 
Industries (SSIs) in the country. While the removal of QRs has exposed the 
SSIs to greater competition, there has not been any surge in imports as a 
consequence of this step. Even after the removal, of QRs, protection to the 
industries is available in the form of raising custom duties upto the bound 
levels, imposing anti-dumping duties, taking safeguards measures in case of 
surge in imports, etc. The Government has also put in place several measures 
to help SSIs become globally competitive.

DR. P.C. ALEXANDER (Maharashtra): Thank you, Madam. 
During the last one fortnight, after the Finance Minister presented the 
Budget in the Lok Sabha, we have been observing the reaction in the country 
to the various proposals, reaction among the consumers, the middle classes, 
the salaried classes, pensioners, agriculturists and manufacturers. No Finance 
Minister can ever expect to have uniform support for all his proposals, but 
judging from the general support that has been extended to his Budget by the 
majority of the people who have chosen to express their views, I think, on the 
whole, the Finance Minister should feel very happy at the reception that has 
been given to his Budget. 
There have been some comments in the Press, and also in this 
House, about the increase in the growth rate that has been projected by the 
Finance Minister. Some people have held a view that a growth rate of six to 
seven per cent, which he has projected, is unrealistic, taking, particularly, into 
account what has happened during the current year. 
There have been also some criticisms about the under-funding of 
certain projects, particularly, the most important project, if I may say so, about 
roads and ports, for which sixty thousand crores of rupees are to be spent in 
three years. I am not going into all these details because I would like to refer 
to three or four other main issues which are of concern to me, and, therefore, I 
feel, should be placed before the House. But I wish to express my personal 
view that a growth rate of six to seven per cent will not be an over ambitious 
target, provided two conditions are fulfilled. One is, the international situation, 
particularly the situation in Iraq, should not worsen and create situations which 
may be outside our control; and the second, of course, is, let us hope, there 
will not be a repetition of the drought situation we experienced during this 
financial year.   Given these two 
220 

[13 March, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
conditions,  I  feel  confident  that  the  growth  rate of 6-7  per cent  is a 
reasonable one and within our reach. 
Madam Deputy Chairperson, I wish to place three main issues before 
the House. The first is about the strategy that has been adopted for poverty 
eradication. The Budget has provided 507 crores of rupees to cover additional 
fifty lakhs of families under the Antyodaya Anna Yojana next year. What I have 
to say on this occasion is, we seem to be just repeating the projects, or the 
basket of projects, which have been under implementation all over the country 
during the past several decades without pausing for some time and finding 
whether the direction that we have taken or given to the country is the right 
one in the situation of 2003 and the years to come. The money that has been 
spent, thousands of crores of rupees that have been spent during the last few 
decades, ever since we started this big fight against poverty, has been well-
spent and is likely to be well-spent in the coming years. I am saying that in 
spite of the commitment which all the Governments in India had, ever since 
Independence shown to the cause of poverty alleviation and eventual 
eradication, in spite of the will that has been displayed by the successive 
Prime Ministers and Governments, we have not succeeded in this programme 
to the extent that we thought we would, though 45-50 years have elapsed 
since the schemes, one after the other have been implemented. I would, 
therefore, suggest that there has to be a critical review of the strategy and the 
questions which are generally raised from the field should be brought to some 
place for sharp attention, discussion, deliberation, and, eventually, decision. 
We are just repeating year after year the schemes which have been 
introduced 20 years ago or 30 years ago. And, the additional schemes which 
have been introduced in the recent years, without bothering whether this type 
of investment, massive investment, in these schemes will take us further in the 
achievement of our goal. Certainly, if we take into account the fact that we are 
still ranked 124 in a list of 174 countries by the UNDP based on HDI, we really 
have to admit the fact that our attempts at poverty eradication or the strategy 
that we have been following for the last 40-45 years has been really not the 
right one. More important than that is that this strategy has brought out a very 
serious new menace, a new hurdle, a very important obstacle to the progress 
of our nation as a whole. We are trying to reduce the disparities between 
communities and communities, castes and castes, but we are not noticing the 
fact that we have created additional disparities in the process between States 
and States and between regions within the States which are
