Houses for Urban Poor in UP 
2626. PROF. M.M. AGARWAL: Will the Minister of URBAN 
DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION be pleased to state: 
(a) the number of houses constructed for urban poor people in the 
State of Uttar Pradesh; 
(b) the number of houses allotted to the people in the State; 
(c) whether Government have formulated any National Action Plan for 
Uttar Pradesh for construction of houses for urban poor; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF URBAN 
DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION (SHRI PON 
RADHAKRISHNAN): (a) and (b) Housing is a State subject. Government of 
India acts only as a facilitator and not as a provider. However, Housing & 
Urban Development Corporation Ltd. (HUDCO), a public sector enterprise 
under this Ministry, provides housing finance to various State agencies for 
housing schemes including those for the weaker sections of the society. 
HUDC© provides housing finances based on demand driven approach. It is 
for State agencies to submit project proposals for the assistance from 
HUDCO, according to their requirements. 
As far as HUDCO is concerned, it has sanctioned 3, 17, 218 residential 
dwelling units in the State of Uttar Pradesh. Out of this, 2,60,278 dwelling 
units (82%) are meant for Economically Weaker Sections and Low-Income 
Group families. 
(c) and (d) The Central Government have adopted the National Housing 
& Habitat Policy, 1998 which envisages Central Government's role as an 
enabler rather than builder. Under the Two Million Housing Programme, in 
Uttar Pradesh, HUDCO has so far sanctioned 1,69,322 dwelling units from 
1998-99 to 2002-2003 for Economically Weaker Sections in urban areas 
against the cumulative target of 1,82,430 dwelling units (annual target is 
36,486 dwelling units).

*362. SHRIMATI BIMBA RAIKAR : W ill the Minister of FINANCE AND 
COMPANY AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government propose to take the sick PSUs out of the 
purview of Board for Industrial and Financial Reconstruction (BIFR) to 
facilitate easy liquidation and faster rehabilitation; 
(b) whether there are plans to scrap the BIFR under the proposed 
Company Law Amendment; 
(c) whether Government have recently issued directives to sick PSUs to 
clear outstanding dues of the employees within 45 days; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF FINANCE AND COMPANY AFFAIRS (SHRI 
JASWANT SINGH): (a) to (d) A Statement is placed on the Table of the 
House. 
Statement 
It is proposed to repeal the Sick Industrial Companies (Special 
Provisions) Act (SICA) and wind up the Board of Industrial and Financial 
Reconstruction (BIFR). An alternative mechanism for liquidation and 
rehabilitation of sick companies has been provided in the Companies Act 
through the Companies (Second Amendment) Act, 2002, which will also 
provide for establishing the National Company Law Tribunal. Under the 
amended Act, an Government company is exempt from the mandatory 
provision for making reference to the Tribunal, other than, with the prior 
approval of the Central or the State Government, as the case may be. 
Administrative Ministries of sick PSUs having outstanding statutory dues 
have been advised to clear them within 45 days, out of their own resources. 
Other loss making and sick PSUs which have outstanding dues, but may not 
have the resources have been advised to expedite clearance of dues by 
disposal of surplus/non-performing a ssets. For enterprises that neither have 
the capacity to clear the dues out of their internal resources nor have 
disposable surplus assets, the Ministries have been advised to frame revival/ 
closure plans.

Closing of Central Water Commission 
†*371. SHRI BASHISTHA NARAIN SI NGH: Will the Minister of WATER 
RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) the main tasks of the Central Water Commission; 
(b) whether it is a fact that the ta sk for development of water resources 
is a subject of the State list and as a result thereof most of the task with regard 
to water resources is executed by the State; and 
(c) the reasons for not closing the same in the public interest while 
utility of commission has become less? 
THE MINISTER OF WATER R ESOURCES (SHRI ARJUN CHARAN 
SETHI): (a) Central Water Commission is an apex technical organization in 
the field of water resources development  in the country and is the main 
technical arm of the Ministry of Wate r Resources. Central Water Commission 
(CWC) is involved with following tasks: 
Resource assessment; macro level planning; project planning including 
hydrological studies, designs, environmental and rehabilitation & resettlement 
issues; project evaluation; extending

RAJYA  SABHA [8 April, 2003] 
advice on planning and design problems, execution of water resources 
development projects and project monitoring; operational flood forecasting & 
dam safety aspects in operation of water resources projects; research and 
development; standardization and documentation; guidance/advisory role in 
report of committees, boards etc. and technical support to different Ministries. 
(b) (i) As per the Seventh Schedule of the Constitution, Entry 
17 of List-ll (State List), "Water that is to say, water supplies, 
irrigation and canals, drainage a nd embankments, water storage and 
water power subject to the provisions of Entry 56 of List I" is with 
the State Governments. 
However, as per Entry 56 of Li st-I (Union List) "Regulation and 
development of inter-state rivers and river valleys to the extent to which such 
regulation and development under the co ntrol of the Union is declared by 
Parliament by law to be expedient in the public interest" is with the Union 
Government. 
From the above it is clear that t he regulation and development of inter-
state rivers is the primary responsibi lity of the Union Government for which 
Central Water Commission extends nece ssary technical support to the 
Government. 
Central Water Commission works on specialized areas of macro level 
planning in water resources development sector which comes under Entry 20 
of List-Ill (Concurrent List) on "Economic and social planning". It performs 
technical tasks with respect to respon sibility of the Central Government on 
Inter-State Boards and Inter-State Water Disputes. 
(c) In view of the present func tions of CWC and constitutional 
provisions as enumerated at (a) and (b) above, it is necessary to 
continue the CWC to discharge sove reign functions of the Union. 
In fact, it will be required to play a more important & pro-active 
role in view of incr easing Inter-State i ssues in river basin 
management, and development needs in water sector of the country 
as well las increasing international emphasis on water related 
issues.

Backlog of vacancies in State Bank of Bikaner and Jaipur 
*380. SHRI GANDHI AZAD: Will t he Minister of FINANCE AND 
COMPANY AFFAIRS be pleased to refer to the reply given in Rajya Sabha to 
Unstarred Question 437 on 23rd April, 2002 and state: 
(a) whether reserved category officers are made members in 
Departmental Promotion Committees by State Bank of Bikaner and Jaipur; 
(b) if so, the details of the last  three years, if not, the reasons 
therefor; and 
(c) the details of steps taken by Bank to fill up Programmer- 
cum-Operators backlog vacancy/post as per DOPT order dated the 
21st January, 2002? 
THE MINISTER OF FINANCE AND COMPANY AFFAIRS (SHRI 
JASWANT SINGH): (a) and (b) State Bank of Bikaner and Jaipur has 
reported that officers belonging to SC/ST were included 
47 

RAJYA SABHA [8 April, 2003] 
in all Departmental Promotion Committees  constituted during the last three

WRITTEN ANSWERS TO UNSTARRED QUESTIONS 
 Adjustment of departure time of small aircrafts 
2627. SHRI DRUPAD BORGOHAIN: Will the Minister of CIVIL 
AVIATION be pleased to state what are the reasons, the departure 
of small aircrafts to different destinations like Imphal, Agartala, 
Dimapur, from Guwahati could not be linked with Delhi-Guwahati 
flights? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF CIVIL AVIATION 
(SHRI SHRIPAD YESSO NAIK): The avail able fleet of four  ATR-42 aircraft 
provides maximum intra North East connectivity. At present, connectivity with 
Delhi-Guwahati flight of Indian Airlines is available to Dimapur and Agartala 
thrice a week. ATR operations to Imphal are yet to commence. However, 
Imphal is connected directly to Delhi via Guwahati twice a week. 
Apart from this, connectivity is also provided from Delhi to stations in 
North-East via Kolkata and vice versa.

2632. SHRI V.V. RAGHAVAN: 
SHRI-J. CHITHARANJAN:

Airlines fares; and

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF CIVIL AVIATION 
(SHRI SHRIPAD YESSO NAIK): (a) and (b ) Indian Airlines has, w.e.f. 26th

in cost of Aviation Turbine Fuel (ATF) and other input costs.

VRS for Al employees 
†2634. SHRIMATI SAVITA SHARDA: Will the Minister of CIVIL 
AVIATION be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have approved the Voluntary Retirement 
Scheme for the employees of Air India to reduce the number of employees; 
(b) if so, the time period in which the said scheme is likely to be 
implemented; 
(c) the number of applications expec ted from the employees for the 
said scheme; and 
(d) the financial burden likely to be borne by the Air India due to this 
scheme? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF CIVIL AVIATION 
(SHRI SHRIPAD YESSO NAIK): (a) to (d) Yes, Sir. The Government has 
approved the VRS for Air India employees subject .to the condition that the 
same shall not deviate in any manner from the DPE's existing guidelines on 
Gujarat pattern of VRS. All permanent  and confirmed employees of the 
Company who are on Indian scales of pay and have completed 10 years of 
service in the Company or who have comp leted 40 years of age on the date of 
closure of the Scheme will be eligible except (i) employees in licensed 
categories 'such as Pilots, Flight Engine ers, Aircraft Engineers; (ii) employees 
in technical & operational categories such as Technical officers, Simulator 
Maintenance Engineers, Service Engineers (Aircraft Non-Licenced), Aircraft 
Equipment Operators, etc.; (iii) employees on contract; (iv) employees who

employees will avail of VRS under the scheme. The financial burden likely to 
be faced by Air India would be about Rs. 57 crores (approx.) for different

Direct flights to the USA and Europe 
2635. SHRI NANDI YELLAIAH: Will t he Minister of CIVIL AVIATION be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether Air India is planning to undertake a major fleet expansion 
by acquiring eight aircrafts on lease to operate direct flights to the USA and 
Europe from various destinations in our country; 
(b) if so, whether Hon'ble Chief Mini ster of A. P. has requested the 
Centre to ensure that adequate number of  flights by Air India from Hyderabad 
are planned to the USA and Europe while finalising the bilaterals with 
countries concerned as a very large nu mber of professionals from Andhra 
Pradesh are working in the USA and Europe; 
(c) if so, whether Government would agree to the request; and 
(d) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF CIVIL AVIATION 
(SHRI SHRIPAD YESSO NAIK): (a) Air India has dry leas ed 9 A310-300 
aircraft and one B747-400 aircraft to undertake flights for growth as well as to 
replace its own old aircrafts like B747-200 and A300-B4. Air India is also in 
the process of dry leasing 10th and 11th A310 in 2003. Air India has 
introduced three flights a week from India to New York via Paris w.e.f. 3rd 
December, 2002. A fourth frequency has been added w.e.f. 30th March, 2003. 
53 

RAJYA SABHA [8 April, 2003] 
In addition, Air India has recommended thrice weekly operations to Frankfurt 
w.e.f. December, 2002. 
(b) Yes, Sir. 
(c) and (d) At present, Hyderabad Airport is not equipped to handle 
B747 aircraft which are being deployed by Air India to operate its services to 
USA. However, Air India serves the Hyderabad-US West Coast market 
through code share flights over the Pacific. Pssengers can travel between 
Hyderabad and Singapore on Air India's own direct services as also on Air 
India's code share services with Silk Air, with convenient connections onward 
to the US West Coast and on Air India's code share flights with Singapore on 
the Singapore/ Los Angeles sector. Air India can also carry passengers 
between Hyderabad and Los Angeles over Kuala Lumpur on its code share on 
Malayasia Airlines Flights Hyderabad-Kuala Lumpur-Los Angeles sector.

Impact of economic recession on industrial sector 
2658. SHRI CO. POULOSE: Will the Minister of FINANCE AND 
COMPANY AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the possibilities of industrial recovery are taking a beating 
with global economic recession continuing unabated; 
(b) whether it is a fact that the grow th of services sector has also been 
adversely effected by the global economic recession; 
(c) whether Government are aware t hat the growth of the services 
sector is contingent upon healthy agricul tural and industrial sectors and with 
the declaration or stagnancy of these sectors the growth of the services 
sector is going to be seriously affected; and 
(d) if so, the steps Government have taken in this regard? 
75 

RAJYA SABHA [8 April, 2003] 
THE MINISTER OF FINANCE AND COMPANY AFFAIRS (SHRI 
JASWANT SINGH): (a) to (d) No, Sir. There is no evidence of any adverse 
impact of global recession on the performa nce of industrial sector as well as 
services sector, rather industry has stimulated overall growth, despite a 
decline in agriculture. As per the latest data on Index of Industrial Production 
(IIP) released by Central Statistical Or ganisation (CSO) industrial production 
registered a growth of 5.5% during Ap ril-January 2002-03 as compared to 
2.6% in the same period last year. Se rvices sector is also growing at a 
reasonably good pace. Exports are also growing at a rate faster than that 
targeted. The latest figures on expor ts for April-February 2002-03 show an 
impressive increase of 16.7% and the manufactured exports constitute around 
80% of total exports from India. Other  indicators of industrial performance 
namely, growth in six infrastructure industries, capital goods, foreign 
exchange reserves and non-food credit  continue to register good growth 
rates. The Government of India has  taken a number of steps including 
enhancement of allocations towards some of the major schemes, which will 
boost demand, especially in construction, housing, steel and cement sectors.

THE MINISTER OF FINANCE AND COMPANY AFFAIRS (SHRI 
JASWANT SINGH): (a) to (c) Yes, Sir.  The Reserve Bank of India, has 
permitted a person resident of India, to open, hold and maintain a Resident 
Foreign Currency (Domestic) Account with an Authorized Dealer in India. 
Foreign exchange acquired from any of the following sources can be kept in 
this account: 
(i) while on visit to any place outside India by way of payment for 
services not arising from any bus iness in or anything done in 
India; or 
(ii) from any person not resident in India and who is on a visit to India, 
as honorarium or gift or for services rendered or in settlement of 
any lawful obligation; or 
(iii) by way of honorarium or gift on a visit to any place outside India; or 
(iv) the unspent amount of foreign exchange acquired by him from an 
authorized person for travel abroad.

2000 or its equivalent in the form of currency notes and/or foreign currency 
travellers cheques. The balance in Resident Foreign Currency (Domestic) 
Account may be used for any purpose permissible under the current foreign 
exchange regulations for resident Indians. 
There is no limit on balances kept in Resident Foreign Currency 
(Domestic) Account. This account will be maintained in the form of a current 
account only with cheque facility.

Tighter accountability norms for banks 
2690. SHRI RAMA MUNI REDDY SIR IGIREDDY: Will the Minister of 
FINANCE AND COMPANY AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the RB I is seriously thinking of bringing

existing laws in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF FINANCE AND COMPANY AFFAIRS (SHRI 
JASWANT SINGH): (a) to (c) The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) had 
constituted an Expert Committee on Lega l Aspects of Bank Frauds under the 
Chairmanship of Dr. N.L. Mitra, Vice Chancellor, National Law University, 
Jodhpur. The Committee submitted its report  to the RBI in two parts. Part I 
dealing with in-house preventive measures and part II dealing with prohibitive 
aspects requiring legislative changes for its implementation. The 
recommendations of the Committee cont ained in part I are Development of 
Best Practice Code (BPC), system of internalisation of BPC, internal check 
and internal control, legal complianc e certification in all transactions 
exceeding a value limit, legal compliance audit, data building on the exercise 
of discretionary power and monitoring th ereof, liability of the accounting and 
auditing profession etc. These recomme ndations were accepted by RBI. All 
Scheduled Commercial Banks were advised to implement them. In part II of 
its report, the Mitra Committee had sugge sted for a separate statute styled 
"Financial Fraud Investigation, Prosecut ion, Recovery and Restoration of 
Property Act, 2001". The Committee has also suggested certain amendments 
to the Indian Penal Code, Criminal Procedure Code and Indian Evidence Act. 
The RBI has accepted the above recommendations and have referred the 
matter to the Government.

uniform across all DPs. The DPs are free to levy their own tariff structure 
based on the services provided by them . The major fee that is charged by 
DPs from their investors is in the form of Annual Account Maintenance 
Charges, which ranges anywhere from Rs. 200/- to Rs. 600/- per annum.

minimum of 30 days' notice is required to  be given by. the DPs to their clients

SHRI LAJPAT RAI: 
Will the Minister of PETROLEUM AND NATURAL GAS be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that with a view to providing subsidy to the 
consumers, the import price of LPG is treated to be basis for assessment of 
quantum thereof; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) the reasons for treating import pric e as basis instead of actual cost 
of production? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PETROLEUM AND 
NATURAL GAS (SHRI SANTOSH GANGWAR): (a) to (c) With the dismantling 
of Administered Pricing Mechanism (APM) in the petroleum sector, the "cost 
plus" mechanism of compensating the oil companies has been done away 
with. Also, oil refining being a continuous process industry with multi product 
output, product wise cost of production is not worked out. 
Since in a free market scenario, the oil companies would need to match 
the prices of an importer of the product at any given location, the methodology 
of import parity pricing has been adopt ed while working out the costings for 
computation of subsidy on domestic LPG.

(a) to (d) The Central Government while expressing its intention to declare the 
Arunachaleshwarar temple in Tiruvannamalai as as of national importance 
under the provisions of Ancient Monuments and Archaeological Sites and 
Remains Act, 1958 has notified the same  in the Official Gazette of India vide 
S.O. No. 1024(E) dated 21.9.2002. 
The Central Government under the pr ovisions of Section 4 of the 
Ancient Monuments and Archaeological Sites and Remains Act, 1958 by 
notification in the Official Gazette of India give two months notice of its 
intention to declare ancient monument as  defined in Section 2 of the Act; any 
structure erection or monument, or any tumulus or place of interment, or any 
cave, rock sculpture, inscription or monolith, which is of historical, 
archaeological or artistic interest and which has been in existence for not less 
than one hundred years to be of national importance. Copy of such notification 
is affixed in a conspicuous place near the monument on the site and remains. 
Any person interested in such ancient monument or site and remains 
may within two months after the issue of the notification, object to the 
declaration of the monument to be of national importance. 
On expiry of two months, the Central Government after considering the 
objection if any, received by it, declare by notification

in the Official Gazette, the said monum ent/site or remains to be of national 
importance.

individuals have filed petition in the High Court of Madras with the prayer to 
grant stay in declaration of Arunachaleshw arar temle in Tiruvannamalai as of 
national importance. SLP (Civil) No . 12443—12447 of 2001 with 13143—
13147 of 2001 between Commissioner, Thiruvannamalai Municipality v/s 
Arunachala Giri Prakakshana Samiti & ot hers is pending before the Hon'ble 
Supreme Court of India wherein the Arch aeological Survey of India has been 
made a party. The Central Government ha ve filed a transfer petition in the 
Supreme Court of India for the transfer of  all the four Writ Petition No. 41227, 
40989, 41142 and 40935 pending before the High Court of Judicature at

Water shortage in developing countries 
2771. SHRIMATI BIMBA RAIKAR: Will the Minister of WATER 
RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether a recent study by FA O(UN) has predicted severe water 
shortage in developing countries; 
(b) whether according to the report the water problem will aggravate to 
the extent that every one country am ong the five developing countries will 
face acute water scarcity; 
(c) whether India participated in the World Water Forum conclave held 
in Kyoto during March 2003; and 
(d) if so, a summary of the deliberations held at the conclave? 
THE MINISTER OF WATER RESOURCES (SHRI ARJUN CHARAN 
SETHI): (a) As per a new study by FAO (UN) titled 'Unlocking the water 
potential of agriculture, published on the eve of the Third World Water Forum 
in Kyoto, it is stated inter-alia that farmers in developing countries will face 
increasing competition for scarce freshwater resources from industry and 
domestic users. It further states that whil e there is no global water crises, the 
serious water and food security problems in some developing countries and 
regions need to be urgently addressed. 
(b) Yes, Madam. 
(c) Yes, Madam. An Indian delegation led by Shri Arjun Charan Sethi, 
Minister of Water Resources participated in the Third World Water Forum held 
in Osaka, Shiga and Kyoto, Japan during March, 2003. 
(d) The 3rd World Water Forum met from 16-23rd March, 2003 in 
Kyoto, Osaka and Shiga, Japan. On this  occasion, two Ministerial meetings, 
namely Irrigation Ministers' meet on "W ater Food and Agriculture" and main 
Ministerial Conference were organized on 21st March and 22-23 March 
respectively. 
During the ministerial meeting on "Water, Food and Agriculture", a 
presentation was made by Secretary (WR) highlighting its achievements in the 
field of agriculture, water resources development 
185 

RAJYA SABHA [8 April, 2003] 
and management alongwith action which needs to be taken to solve 
agriculture water issues in our country. In this regard, need for building dams 
to augment water supplies for food security and poverty alleviation as well as 
imperative need for transfer of water from surplus areas to deficit areas was 
expressed. A Ministerial declarati on, which was earlier negotiated after 
prolonged discussions by senior officers, was adopted on 21st March, 2003. It 
outlines a plan for action to modernize and improve agriculture use, increase 
water prodcutivity, promote better governance, consider environmental 
aspects, undertake research and deve lopment and foster international 
cooperation. 
In the main ministerial declaration adopted in the final plenary session 
on 23rd March, statement was made on  General Policy, Water Resources 
Management and Benefit Sharing, Safe Drinking Water and Sanitation, Water 
for Food and Rural Development, Water Pollution Prevention and Ecosystem 
Conservation and Disaster Mitigation and Risk Management. 
Minister (WR) chaired one of t he five sub-groups session of the 
ministerial conference where issue of  "Water Resources Management and 
Benefit Sharing* was discussed. This session was attended by 
Ministers/representatives of  62 countries, one region and eight International 
Organizations. 
In this sub-group meeting, the nee d to develop dams for irrigation, 
storages, flood control and hydro-electric  energy with due consideration to 
environmental and social impact as well as sound resettlement plans was 
brought out. It also underscored the need for international financial assistance 
for capacity building & technology transfer. It also urged the need for good 
governance and confidence-building measures and emphasized the 
requirement to increase the use of innovative and appropriate technologies 
such as desalination and re-use of treated water. 
Apart from the Senior Officials' Me etings for finalization of Draft 
Declaration and the Ministerial Conferen ce in which the Declarations were 
adopted, there were many Sessions, some of them running parallel, organized 
at Kyoto, Shiga and Osaka.

122 countries for their water quality as also their ability and 
187 

RAJYA  SABHA [8 April, 2003] 
commitment of improving its quality,  as revealed in the World Water 
Development Report; 
(b) if so, the details in this regard; and 
(c) if so, what long-term steps Gove rnment propose to adopt regarding 
adequacy of water supply in the country and improving its quality? 
THE MINISTER OF WATER RESOURCES (SHRI ARJUN CHARAN 
SETHI): (a) and (b) Yes, Sir. As per  the 'United Nations World Water 
Development Report-Water for people, Water for Life', India has been ranked 
120th among 122 selected nations in the world in terms of quality of water. 
Belgium is at 122th rank. The report states that the indicators like the 
widespread occurance of poor water quality, the diversion of water from 
natural aquatic ecosystems and the emerging problems with ground water 
recharge were noted for indications of relative water quality. 
(c) Water being a State subject, water resources schemes including the 
schemes to overcome the shortage of water resources are formulated, 
planned, executed and funded by the c oncerned State Governments. To help 
the State Governments in their effort s to harness the water from natural 
resources and accelerate creation of irrigation potential by early completion of 
ongoing schemes, Government of India has launched Accelerated Irrigation 
Benefits Programme (AIBP) since 1996-97 to provide central loan assistance. 
Government of India is promoting rainwater harvesting through 
Watershed Mangement Programme, artificial recharge of ground water rooftop 
rainwater harvesting under the sector reform project of Accelerated Rural 
Water Supply Programme under the Ministry of Rural Development, for which 
technical and financial assistance is provided to the State Governments and 
other implementing agencies. The Governm ent of India also assists the State 
Governments by providing financial assistance under Accelerated Rural Water 
Supply Programme (ARWSP) for rural drinking water and under Command 
Area Development Programme to increase efficiency in utilisation of irrigation 
water. Central Ground Water Board has also taken up a 
188 

[8 April, 2003] RAJYA   SABHA 
Central Sector Scheme on "Studies of Recharge to Ground Water" on pilot 
basis. 
For meeting future requirements of water, as a long term measure, 
National Water Development Agency have formulated National Perspective 
Plan for water resources development which envisages interlinking between 
various Peninsular rivers and Himalayan rivers for transfer of water from 
surplus basins to water deficit basins which will accrue benefits of drinking 
water supply, irrigation, hydro-power, flood control, navigation, fisheries, 
salinity and pollution control etc. 
Several steps have been taken for improvement/restoration of quality of 
water bodies in the country and some of them are : 
(i) Ensuring industries, located on the banks of rivers and lakes, set 
up the requisite pollution control facilities. 
(ii) Issuance of Directives to the defaulting industries for preventing 
discharge to untreated waste water into water bodies. 
(iii) Formulation and implementation of National River and Lake 
Conservation Plan for restoration of water quality of the rivers 
and lakes.

NEED FOR CLEARANCE OF PENDING IRRIGATION PROJECTS 
OF ANDHRA PRADESH WITH THE CENTRAL GOVERNMENT 
DR. T. SUBBARAMI REDDY (Andhra Pradesh): Three proposals (1) 
Janjhvati; (2) Velingonda and (3) Hyderabad Water Supply Scheme are 
pending with the Central Government for approval since 1992,  1997 and 
1998. 
210 

[8 April, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
1. Janjhvati Project: 
This project envisages to utilize 4 TMC of water of river Janjhvati to 
provide irrigation in 24,636 acres of land in vlzianagaram district. The project 
was formulated on the basis of an inter-State agreement signed between the 
States of Orissa and Andhra Pradesh in  1976 to utilize waters of Janjhvati 
river. 
2. Velingonda Project: 
Velingonda project envisages to draw 40 TMC of flood water of the 
river Krishna from Srisailam reservoir through the Naliamala hills to provide 
irrigation in 4.38 lakh acres of land in  the drought prone area of Prakasam 
district.  The Ministry of Environment and Forests has given its clearance. 
3. Hyderabad Water supply and sanitation project: 
To provide adequate drinking water to a population of 50 lakhs in 
Hyderabad, the State Government formulated a scheme of lifting 16.5 TMC of 
water from the foreshore of Nagarjunasagar reservoir on the inter-State river 
Krishna. This scheme will be funded by the World Bank and requires a 
clearance from CWC. The water for this scheme is proposed by AP for 
utilization from out of its allocation under KWDT award. 
As all these projects are impor tant and are pending with the 
Government of India for long, hence requ ire early clearance, so that these 
projects are implemented for the benefit of people of Andhra Pradesh. Thank 
you. 
DEMAND FOR WITHDRAWAL OF TEN PER CENT EXCISE DUTY 
ON POWERLOOM FABRICS 
SHRI P.G. NARAYANAN (Tamil Nadu): The powerloom industry in 
Tamil Nadu is in a very bad state of affairs. The latest blow has come due to 
the imposition of 10 per cent excise  duty on powerloom fabric which was 
recently announced in the current Budget. 
The powerloom owners in the State were already undergoing an 
ordeal, in view of the recessionary trend and a sluggish demand for their 
products. In the present trend to boost the powerloom sector industries and to 
improve the means of livelihood of mil lions of people, the Centre should 
seriously consider the withdrawal of new excise levy. The powerloom 
industries should be permitted to adopt the optional excise duty which is in 
vogue now.   If it is not possible due to the prevailing economic 
211 

RAJYA SABHA        [8 April, 2003] 
scenario, at least, those whose turnover is less than Rs.1 crore should be 
exempted from the new levy. 
In view of the prevailing circumst ances and the difficulties faced by 
the powerloom sector, the Chief Minister of Tamil Nadu has written a letter to 
the hon. Prime Minister to reconsider the new excise levy at the earliest. 
I, therefore, strongly urge upon t he Government to withdraw the 
excise duty of 10 per cent on powerloom fabrics, at the earliest, so as to revive 
the powerloom sector and render justice.   Thank you.

NEED FOR CHANGING NORMS FOR CENTRALLY-SPONSORED 
ACCELERATED URBAN WATER SUPPLY PROGRAMME 
SHRIMATI SHABANA AZMI (Nominated): Sir, it is a matter of great 
shame that five decades after independence we still have not been able to 
give drinking water to all our people. My Special Mention is about the 
Centrally-Sponsored Accelerated Water Supply Programme in Maharashtra 
This scheme is a Centrally-s ponsored programme. As per 1991 
Census, there were 79 towns having less than 20,000 population in 
Maharashtra. Thirty-six proposals were sent to the Union Government. The 
Union Government approved 20 proposals. Out of that, water supply has 
started under 13 schemes and the work on the remaining 7 is in progress. 
The Government of India has not approved the remaining 16 
schemes, although the State Government  has already started the work on 
these schemes. Now, these schemes have been omitted from the AUWSP. 
Only three schemes have been approved in the month of January, 2003. 
The State Government of Maharasht ra had suggested the following 
changes:- 
Norms of population to be raised from 20,000 to 1 lakh Per capita 
cost to be raised from Rs. 1,000 to Rs.2,400 minimum. Raising the 
water supply limit from 70 litres to 100 litres per day per person. 
The above changes were discussed at the meeting held on 4 th and 
5th July, 1996 and all the Chief Mini sters of States had recommended the 
changes. 
The Maharashtra Chief Minister has been writing letters to the Prime 
Minister of India on the subject. The Working Group constituted by the 
Government of India in August, 1996 had also recommended changes in the 
norms.    The proposals were discussed at a meeting held under the

of India, on 8 th June, 2001. The Government of India has not yet given 
approval to the proposed changes in the norms.

norms suggested by Maharashtra Government, which had been supported by 
all the Chief Ministers, so that t he schemes can be implemented by the 
Government of Maharashtra.  Thank you. 
NEED TO TACKLE THE SPREAD OF MYSTERY DISEASE SEVERE 
ACUTE RESPIRATORY SYNDROME (SARS) 
SHRIMATI N.P.DURGA (Andhra Prades h) : Sir, my special mention 
is about panic over spread of myster y disease, SARS. A new disease known 
as Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome and closely resembles influenza is 
suspected to be a mutant. It starts with high fever, sore throat and cough, but 
has been found to turn fatal when it develops into full-fledged pneumonia. The 
city of Hong Kong has been hit with SARS claiming maximum number of lives 
there and in China also. This disease has spread to South-East Asian 
countries creating a panic like situat ion. It has spread to Canada, Brazil and 
other countries also. So far. this virus has infected 2,300 people in 14 
countries. About 80 people have died. Since China is our neighbouring 
country, we have to be on our guard. Up till now, doctors and WHO could not 
find a diagnose to this disease. 
This has affected business and there is a slump in tourist arrivals. 
This is having a negative im pact on the business. It is sad to learn that WHO 
had little information on what causes SAR S. I think the Government of India 
have taken some measures to alert our airports to check the suspected 
passengers coming from South-East Asian countries and alerted hospitals and 
immunology institutions for treating patients. We have to educate the people of 
India that the disease will not spread if we maintain good hygiene and make 
everyone aware of it through good health education through electronic and 
print media. God forbid, if such a dis ease strikes our country, the Government 
of India should be prepared to tackle it on a war footing.

SHRIMATI N.P. DURGA (Andhr a Pradesh): Madam Deputy 
Chairperson, it gives me great pleasure to speak on this small piece of 
legislation, moved by the hon. Mini ster for Consumer Affairs, Food and 
Public distribution. The Bill is brou ght before us to amend the Essential 
Commodities Act to plug the loopholes with the help of which some of the 
sugar mills are indulging in malpractices and are selling more sugar in the 
open market than prescribed by the Government, resulting in decline in the 
payment of price to sugarcane growers. The problem arose because the sugar 
release mechanism is governed not directly by the Essential Commodities Act, 
but by the Sugar (Control) Order, 1966.  Taking advantage 
228 

[8 April, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
of this, some of the mills went to c ourt and got decree in their favour under 
article 19 and 14 of the Constitution because clauses 4 and 5 of the Sugar 
(Control) Order are not in conformity with articles 14 and 19 (1) (9) of the 
Constitution. I welcome the inclusion of new clauses, 3(d) and 3(e), in the Act, 
which plugs this loophole and helps the producers of sugarcane to get the 
minimum support price decided by the Government. This is the simple 
amendment that the Government has brought before the House for its 
approval.   It is a good decision. 
But, at the same time, the sugar mills are also facing a tot of 
problems. We all know that sugar i ndustry is the second-largest agro-based 
industry in the country, and the largest industry located in rural areas. We 
have more than half a thousand sugar factories in the country, and the annual 
production is around 190 lakh tonnes. As  of today, the sugar mills are facing 
compound losses to the tune of Rs. 5,500 crores. This industry is facing losses 
for the last three years because of exce ssive production. One of the problems 
that this industry is facing is with regard to the minimum support price of 
sugarcane, which is going up year after year. Tax, power and water charges, 
transportation charges are all going up and the result is that  the production 
cost of sugar is also going up. The other problem is the technology that we are 
using is obsolete. For this, we have to find out some innovative techniques so 
as to reduce the cost of production. If yo u look at other countries, the cost of 
production of one tonne sugar comes to Rs. 9,975/-. whereas in India it is Rs. 
13,700/-! So, there is. nearly, a differ ence of Rs. 4,oooA per tonne in the 
production cost alone. I agree that the countries such as Brazil, USA, Japan, 
and some European countries are giving subsidy. But, the technology that has 
been adopted there is far more advanc ed than the technology that we are 
using here. So. I would like to know from the hon. Minister what his Ministry is 
doing to reduce the cost of production of sugar. 
The other worrying issue is that the exports are also coming down. I 
will just give one example. Last year, we had exported about 11.5 million 
tonnes of sugar, whereas this year, the exports slumped to 10 million tonnes. 
So, I would like to know from the hon. Minister how is he going to export more 
sugar to other countries and deal with the exorbitant import duties imposed by 
some of the developed countries? I would also like to know from the hon. 
Minister the impact of Iraq War on our ex port of sugar. I suggest that when 
other countries are imposing more and more import duty, why can't India do 
the same and save our sugar mills, which are on

reduce sugar imports and, thereby, redu ce piling up of sugar stocks in the

is demanding for retaining tax on sugar, excise duty, central cess on sugar and 
excise duty on molasses for a short period of one year, in the light of the 
pathetic condition in which the sugar indus try is passing through? If yes; what 
is the Government doing In this regard? 
Finally, I wish to bring to the notice of the hon. Minister that Brazil and 
other developed countries are allowing about 10-15 per cent ethanol to be 
mixed with petrol, whereas we are allowing only 5 per cent of ethanol to be

I would also like to know what the Ministry is doing with regard to

I want the hon. Minister to respond to the queries raised by me.

SHRI P.G. NARAYANAN (Tamil Na du): Madam Deput y Chairman, 
the Essential Commodities Act, 1955 provides for maintaining or increasing 
supplies of essential commodities or for securing their equitable distribution 
and availability at fair prices. The Central Government may issue orders 
regulating or prohibiting the producti on, supply and distribution of such 
essential commodities in trade and commerce. The present Bill aims to 
amend Section 3 of the Act. The new Sections 3(d) and 3(e) have been 
introduced. This amendment has to be  read with Sugar Control Order, 1966. 
This amendment has been brought forth keeping in mind the policy of partial 
control of sugar since 1966 and allocating a portion of sugar as levy sugar for 
the Public Distribution System. We ar e very well aware that the Central 
Government has adopted a regulated release mechanism for release of levy 
free sugar, that is. free sale sugar by issuing orders under the Sugar Control 
Order, 1966. As per new amendments, a ccording to the directions of the 
Central Government, a producer can import, export, dispose of, deliver or 
remove any kind of sugar from the bounded godowns of the factory. While 
implementing this Section, we should see to it that it does not affect the 
pledging of such sugar by the producer in favour of any scheduled bank. 
Madam, the Sugar Control Order was la st amended in June 1999. Clause 4 
and clause 5 of the said Order empowered the Government to give direction 
to the producer, on lines similar to the new amendment, that is, Sections 3(d) 
and 3(e) of the Essential Commodities B ill. I very well understood the recent 
challenge the Government is facing to the regulated release mechanism in the 
courts, which has led to the difficulties in its operation. Due to the difficulties in 
operating there, there is a sharp decline in the sugar prices also, which in turn, 
affects the capacity of t he producer to pay cane prices to the sugarcane 
growers. Please, ensure that these pr ovisions will definitely safeguard the 
interests of the sugarcane growers,  producers and general public. The 
present amendments are aimed at re-sta bilising the market prices of sugar 
and to overcome the difficulties

Madam, the thrust of this Bill relates to two special aspects with 
regard to the procedure for elections to the Members of the Council of States 
i.e. the Rajya Sabha. We have since 1951 had a firm system where to be 
eligible under section 3 of the Represent ation of the People Act, to contest for 
the election for the Rajya Sabha, one has to be an elector of that State; and 
under section 19 of the Act, in order to be an elector of the State, you have to 
be a person ordinarily resident in that State. Now, several features over the 
functioning of this election system hav e come to notice. In a large number of 
cases, political parties which send repr esentatives from various States, have 
sent a person, who traditionally was not resident in that State, but for the 
purposes of election to the Rajya Sabha, got enrolled as elector in that 
particular State. If we do recollect, about six - seven years ago, there was a 
large controversy whether this practice now requires to be changed, as far as 
the legal system is concerned. We tried to develop a consensus amongst 
political -parties. Some of the political  parties took a particular view that a 
change, perhaps, is now required. Some people still had reservations about 
this. One of the points of criticism which was made against this proposal was 
that this may perhaps affect the spirit of federalism, which is otherwise inherent 
in the fact that it is only an elector of a State who gets elected from that 
particular State. Under the existing syst em or the proposed system, it is the 
Members of the Legislative Assembly of the State who are the electors. It is 
their option whom they choose to elect; who they feel can best represent the 
interests of the State. As against th is, several arguments have been given, 
which I present before the hon. House, as to why this system requires now to 
be altered. One of the first reasons why it requires to be altered is, because in 
the matter of its actual implementation, a breach too frequently was witnessed. 
Therefore, political parties wanted to come to an honest

assessment of the situation and come to a conclusion that this, perhaps, now 
requires to be altered itself. The second, under our constitutional scheme, 
under article 19 (1)(e), a person has a right to reside anywhere in the country. 
So, a person who wants to change his residence -- there may be cases where 
people maintain more than one residence, for reasons of business -- for other 
reasons of family, people may be residing in more than one place 
simultaneously. Therefore, this, perhaps may not be in a position to deal with 
such situations, the existing situation. The third reason which was also besides 
the factor of multiple residence is t hat there may be some States where even 
the ruling party or a ruling combination may be unrepresented completely, as 
far as the Lok Sabha is concerned; ma ybe unable to bring Members to the 
Upper House who are among the usual resi dents of that Stat e. Therefore, in 
order to make sure that in the Govern ment also there is representation of 
those States, there may be a compelli ng necessity to get some ordinary 
resident of that State elected from so me other State. It has happened in the 
past; it has happened even today. T here is one particular State which was 
completely unrepresented, otherwise, as far as NDA. is concerned, both in the 
Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha. Therefor e, Members got elected from other 
parts of the country, in order to make  sure that those States also got a 
representation in the Council  of Ministers. With thes e facts, the Government 
had introduced this Bill. There were two views even before the Standing 
Committee. 
The second component of this Bill is with regard to the methodology 
of casting their votes amongst the Legislative Assemblies, as far as election to 
the Council of States is concerned. Currently, we have a system where parties 
put up candidates. But we have several ca ses- I have a list of cases, in the

not very happy for a democracy, which have crept into the polling system. 
Cross-votings have taken place for reasons which are not entirely political. It 
happened in Maharashtra, it happened in  some other States also where

crime and terrorism.

activities.

*388. SHRI P. PRABHAKAR REDDY : Will the Minister of POWER be 
pleased to state what are the steps Gove rnment have taken to ensure adequate 
power supply in Delhi and to narrow the gap between the demand and the 
supply of power in the coming months in the Capital? 
THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI ANANT GANGARAM GEETE): A 
Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
Supply and distribution of power in Delhi is in the purview of 
Government of NCT of Delhi. However, electricity being a concurrent 
subject, Ministry of Power, Government of India reviews power supply 
position in the National Capital, Delhi from time to time and provides 
assistance, whenever required, to augmen t availability of power. It has been 
ascertained that as against the anticipated peak demand of 3200 MW in April, 
2003 and 3700 MW in July/August, 2003, the supply of 
24 

[9 April, 2003] RAJYA   SABHA 
power has been arranged from various sources in the range of 3300 MW-
3800 MW in the different months. (The peak demand registered during the 
summer of 2002 was 3347 MW). 
The following steps have been taken and assistance provided by the 
Government of India to improve the availability of power in Delhi during the 
ensuing summer months: 
1. 197 MW has been allocated from the unallocated quota of Central 
Generating Stations in Northern Re gion to Delhi with effect from 
1st April, 2003. 
2. Allocation of entire 15% unallocat ed quota (66 MW) in Rajasthan 
Atomic Power Project (RAPP-B) Units III & IV has been made 
from mid-April, 2003. 
3. Arrangements have been tied up by National Thermal Power 
Corporation Limited (NTPC) for procuring liquid fuel to make up 
for any shortfall in supply of gas fuel for its gas based power plants 
in the Northern Region of which Delhi is also a beneficiary. 
4. No shut down of generating units in Northern Region has been 
planned by NTPC during May-August, 2003. 
5. Arrangements have been made through Power Trading Corporation 
(PTC) for purchase of 320 to 390 MW from various sources. 
As per information ascertained from Government of NCT Delhi/ Delhi 
Transco Ltd. (DTL), the following steps have been/are being taken to 
augment and ensure reliability of power supply in Delhi. 
1. Commissioning of 400 KV Bamnouli-Ballabgarh double circuit line 
by 30th April, 2003 to complete 400 KV transmission ring around 
Delhi. 
2. Addition of 900 MVA transformation capacity in Delhi system upto 
May, 2003 out of which 400 MVA has already been added. 
3. Arrangements tied up with concerned agencies for procuring liquid 
fuel to make up shortfall in supply of gas to its gas based power 
plants. 
25 

RAJYA SABHA [9 April. 2003] 
4. DTL and Distribution Companies augmenting the availability of 
shunt capacitors in Delhi Power System including rectification of 
defective capacitors so as to improve the voltage profile. 
5. DTL/Distribution Companies to launch campaigns to promote 
energy efficiency and energy conservation measures. 
6. DTL has made arrangements for procuring additional 80-440 MW 
in the different months from Hi machal Pradesh State Electricity 
Board (HPSEB) bilaterally. 
7. DTL to tie up additional 100-150 MW from other States. 
8. Arrangements made to ensure that no planned shut-down is required 
for maintenance of generating units between May to August, 2003.

these regions; and

(SHRI HARIN PATHAK): (a) and (b) Yes, Sir. In India, there is no large scale 
organized cultivation of illicit opium and cannabis. The country is traditionally 
a licit cultivator of opium poppy, which is grown in Central India under the

destroyed and action initiated against the persons involved in such activities.

been addressed by the Narcotics Control Bureau (NCB) to constitute

PTS for power 
2886. SHRI GHULAM NABI AZAD: Will the Minister of POWER be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware that one of the pre-requisites for any 
Public Transport System (PTS) is the availability of power or fuel; 
(b) if so, whether Government have ample resources to ensure the 
necessary power supply or fuel supply; and 
(c) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF POWER (SHRIMATI 
JAYAWANTI MEHTA): (a) Electricity is consumed by Railways for traction. 
Apart from motor spirit and High Speed Diesel (HSD), Compressed Natural 
Gas (CNG) and Liquified Petroleum Gas (LPG) have also been permitted for 
use in public transport system. 
(b) The electricity consumption of the Indian Railways for traction is only 
2.2% of the country's total consumption.. State Electricity Boards/ Power 
Companies from whom Railways purchas e electricity for traction purposes 
accord highest priority for supplying power. The existing refining capacity of 
116.07 Million Tonnes per annum is more than the estimated current annual 
demand of around 104 Million Tonnes of petroleum products. The import 
dependence in oil sector is of around 69%. 
(c) There is no power cut to public transport system or shortage of 
transporation fuels i.e. petrol, diesel and aviation transport fuel.

Private power projects 
2889. SHRI MURLI DEORA: Will the Minister of POWER be pleased 
to state: 
(a) the total number of private power projects existing at present in the 
country, State-wise; 
(b) the number of these projects sanctioned by Central Electricity 
Authority till date and by when these plants will start generating power in 
addition to (a) above; 
(c) the manner by which the power produced by these private plants will be 
utilized; and 
(d) the assistance provided by Government to these plants, State-wise? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF POWER (SHRIMATI 
JAYAWANTI MEHTA): (a) A total of 52 private power projects are presently 
existing in the country.The State-wise break-up is Himachal Pradesh-2, Gujarat-9, 
Maharashtra-8, Goa-1, Andhra Pradesh-5, Kerala-3, Karnataka-6, Tamil 
Nadu-5, Jharkhand-1, West Bengal-9, Assam-2 and Andaman & Nicobar-1 
.These also include the power projects of private licensee companies which 
were in existence even prior to announcement of the policy in 1991 to 
encourage greater private sector participation in the power sector. 
(b) Out of a total of 61 private power projects accorded techno-eco-nomic 
clearance (TEC) by the Central Electricity  Authority (CEA), 16 projects have 
so far been commissioned, which are included in the projects mentioned under 
reply to (a) above. Of the remaining 45 projects, 4 are no longer being pursued 
through private sector by the respective States. The commissioning of the 
balance 41 projects depends upon tying up  of the required inputs/clearances 
(including financial closure) by the project developers. 
(c) Power from the private power project s is generally fed into the State 
Grid for further distribution. 
(d) Government of India (Gol) has been facilitating implementation of 
151 

RAJYA  SABHA [9 April, 2003] 
these projects in trying up the required inputs/clearances though no financial 
assistance is being provided for privat e sector power projects. However, Gol 
has provided counter guarantee to 6 out of 8 identified private sector power 
projects viz. the 740 MW Dabhol (Phase-I) and 1082 MW Bhadrawati power 
projects in Maharashtra, 216 MW Jegurupadu (Phase-I) and 1040 MW 
Visakhapatnam projects in Andhra Pradesh, 250 MW Neyveli-Zero Unit project 
in Tamil Nadu and 420 MW lb Valley project (Units 3 & 4) in Orissa with to 
provide financial comfort to the investors and their lenders.Three of the projects 
viz. Dabhol (Phase-I), Jegurupadu (Phase-I) and Neyveli-Zero Unit having a total 
capacity of 1206 MW have been commissioned. Counter guarantees given for 
the Bhadrawati and Visakhapatnam projects have lapsed due to inability of 
the projects to comply with the required conditions. Counter guarantee given 
to the lb Valley project has also, lapsed since the project parameters have been 
changed with the new capacity being 500 MW (Units 5 & 6). 
One of the projects ( viz., Godavari CCGT in Andhra Pradesh) withdrew 
the request for a Gol counter guarantee. Counter guarantee could not be issued 
to the Mangalore project in Karnatak a since the State Government did not 
accept the prescribed conditions.

TEXTILES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the US and the European Union have been applying the 
provisions of the Multi-Fibre Agreement differently among the developing 
countries while importing textile and apparel products; 
(b) if so, whether the MFA, which came into the force from 1974, has 
sought to prop up Chinese exports much higher than those from India before 
imposing quotas on them; 
(c) if so, the steps Government propose to take in this regard; 
(d) whether the question has been taken up by India with both US and EU; 
and 
(e) if so, their reaction thereto? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF TEXTILES (SHRI 
BASANGOUDA R. PATH): (a) to (e) Till December 31,1994, the exports of 
textiles to certain developed countries including U.S.A., member c ountries of 
the European Union and Canada had been governed by bilateral textile agreements 
entered into between India and these countries under the aegis of the Multi-Fibre 
Arrangement (MFA), outside the rules of the General Agreement on Tariffs 
and Trade (GATT). With effect from January 1,190S. the quantitative 
restrictions (import quotas) in the bilateral agreements under the MFA, are being 
governed by the Agreement on Textiles and Clothing (ATC) contained in the 
Final Act of the Uruguay Round nego tiations of the GATT. Presently, our 
textiles and clothing exports f ace restraints in U.S.A., European Union and 
Canada. 
One of the central elements of the Agreement on Textiles and Clothing (ATC) 
is the four-stage process for the progressive integration of textiles and clothing 
products as specified in the Annex to the ATC into GATT 1994 over a ten-year 
transition period. The integration process has however not led to any meaningful 
removal of quotas by the restraining countries so far. India has raised the issue of 
lack of progressive liberalization in international trade in textilec bilaterally and 
also at the World Trade Organization. In accordance with ATC, all the textile 
quotas would be phased out and textile sector fully integrated into WTO by 1st 
January 2005. 
195 

RAJYA  SABHA [9 April, 2003] 
There is no material available to infer that MFA has sought to prop up 
Chinese exports much higher than those of India before imposing quotas on 
them.

2933. SHRI RUMANDLA RAMACHANDRAYYA: Will the Minister of 
TEXTILES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether India together with 16 other developing countries including 
China has joined hands to fight the protectionism being practised by the EU 
and US in the area of textiles;

the WTO, the countries have sought protection from unjustified recourse to 
trade remedy actions; 
203 

RAJYA SABHA [9 April, 2003] 
(c) if so, the nations which have jointly submitted the report; and 
(d) the reaction of the WTO on this issue? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF TEXTILES (SHRI 
BASANGOUDA R. PATH): (a) to (c) With respect to anti-dumping practices, 
the Ministerial Conference in Doha had mandated negotiations aimed at clarifying 
and improving disciplines under the Anti-dumping Agreement while 
preserving the basic concepts, principa ls and effectiveness of the Agreement 
and its instruments and objectives, and taking into consideration the needs of 
developing and least-developed participants. In the initial phase of the 
negotiations, participants will indicate the provisions, including disciplines on 
trade distorting practices that they seek to clarify and improve in the 
subsequent phase. 
In accordance with th e above Ministerial mandate, India along with 
Bangladesh, Brazil, the People's Republic  of China, Colombia, Costa Rica, 
Egypt, Guatemala, Hong Kong, China, Indonesia,  Korea, Macao, China, 
Maldives, Pakistan, Paraguay, Peru, Thailand and Vietnam had submitted a 
proposal to the WTO's Negotiating Group on Rules, the purpose of which is as 
under:— 
(i) To share developing countries experience as regards antidumping 
activity affecting their exports of textiles and cloth-ing—the largest 
industrial export sector for them. 
(ii) To spell out developing countries needs in the area, it may be 
emphasized in this connection that the Ministerial mandate specifically 
requires that "the needs of developing and least-developed 
participants" be taken into account. 
(iii) To illustrate one of the par ticularly important aspects of anti-
dumping—initiations—as a matter for improved discipline. 
(d) The negotiations on the Anti-dumping Agreement and the Agreement on 
Subsidies and Countervailing Measures are being undertaken in the Negotiating 
Group on Rules (NG Rules). Five meetings of the NG Rules have so far been 
held and three more meetings are scheduled prior to the Cancum Ministerial 
meeting. The negotiations are currently in the first phase during which the WTO 
Member countries are identifying issues for negotiations in the second phase.

Rehabilitation of Camp Inmates of kokrajhar District In Assam 
(SHRI URKHAO GWARA BRAHMA (Assam): Madam, my Special mention

financial crunch. Unless the Central Government provides the required amount of 
money, the total rehabilitation of these people is not possible. At present, the 
Centre provides money on the reimburs ement basis, and it is clubbed with 
security-related expenditure. There is a delay in the process of reimbursement 
also. On the other hand, till date, the State Government has been able to 
provide only Rs. 2.00 crores. So, in this situation, on humanitarian grounds, the 
Centre should sanction the required amount as one-time grant to accelerate 
the rehabilitation process. At the same time, to help the rehabilitation process, 
the Centre is also requested to sanc tion as many as 33,000 houses under 
Indira Awas Yojana so that poor people staying in relief camps can carry on 
normal life in their respective places. In the case of the cyclone affected people 
of Orissa, the Government of India took some initiative. The case of the riot-
affected people of Kokrajhar district of Assam also should be considered as a 
special case; and this act of kindness may help the district administration to 
complete the process within the short period.

Rs. 150 crores.

Recommendations of sixth World Hindi Conference 
†*401. SHRI BASHISTHA NARAIN SINGH: Will the Minister of 
EXTERNAL AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) the recommendation of the Sixth World Hindi Conference organised 
in London; 
(b) whether these recommendations have been implemented fully, if so, 
the details thereof; 
(c) if not, the reasons therefor; and 
(d) What would be the terms of reference of the next conference? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF EXTERNAL 
AFFAIRS (SHRI DIGVIJAY SINGH): (a) to  (d) A statement is laid on the 
table of the House. 
† Original notice of the question was received in Hindi.

[10 April, 2003] RAJYA   SABHA 
Statement 
(a) to (d) The VI World Hindi Conf erence was organised at London 
from 14th to 18th September, 1999. The major recommendations of the 
Conference included, that Mahatma Gandhi International Hindi University 
should be developed as an international centre of Hindi learning. The 
Governments of India and Mauritius should expedite the process of 
establishment of World Hindi Secretaria t in Mauritius. Serious efforts should 
be made towards recognition of Hindi as one of the official languages in the 
UN. Our Missions/Posts should liaise with the people of Indian origin so that 
teaching of Hindi is promoted in the countries of their accreditation and Hindi 
books and other teaching material should  be provided to them as required. 
Hindi learning should be facilitated with the use of the advancement of 
information technology. 
The Government made every effort to implement the recommendations. 
The Mahatma Gandhi International Hindi University has been established and 
is functioning as an international centre of Hindi tearing. After a 
Memorandum of Understanding having been signed between India and 
Mauritius, the Mauritian National Assembly has passed a Bill on 16th 
November, 2002 for setting up of the Secretariat. A high-level Committee has 
also been set up under the chairmanship  of External Affairs. Minister on the 
subject of recognising Hindi as one of the Official Languages in the UN. Our 
Missions/Posts are maintaining close liaison with the Hindi scholars/ 
organisations in the countries of their accreditation with a view to support and 
enrich their Hindi propagating activities. Hindi learning material, books, CDs, 
software are being catered to them by  the Ministry, as per their demands. 
Different software to facilitate Hind i teaching have been developed by C-
DAC, Pune, such as, LILA PRABODH and PRAVEEN and these are also 
being used for Hindi learning. 
The VII World Hindi Conference is being organised at Paramaribo 
(Surinam) from 5th to 9th June, 2003. "World Hindi - Challenges of the new 
Century" is the theme of the VII World Hindi Conference. Emphasis will be 
on exploring the ways and means of popularising the use of Hindi among 
foreigners, particularly people of Indian origin, facilitating the learning of 
Hindi using modem methods and

rich legacy of Hindi language and literature.

reputed Public Relations firm to do the lobbying on behalf of the Indian IT 
Industry.

Slashing of rates by cellular companies 
*407.  SHRI BHAGATRAM MANHAR: 
SHRI RAJU PARMAR: 
Will the Minister of COMMU NICATIONS AND INFORMATION 
TECHNOLOGY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that cellular companies in the country have 
slashed their rates for mobile users; 
(b) if so, what are the rates/schemes at present being offered by these 
cell phone operators; and 
(c) whether the rates of MTNI and BSNL are very high as compared 
to the cell phone operators, and if so , the comparative rates of cell phone 
operators vis-a-vis the landline operators namely MTNL/BSNL/VSNL? 
THE MINISTER OF COMMUNICATIONS AND INFORMATION 
TECHNOLOGY (SHRI ARUN SHOURIE): (a) to (c) A Statement is laid on 
the Table of the House. 
19 

RAJYA  SABHA [10 April, 2003] 
Statement 
(a) and (b) Sir, the Telecom Regulatory Authority of India (TRAI) is 
responsible for fixation of tariffs fo r telecom services including Cellular 
Mobile Telephone Service (CMTS) in the country. Tariff for CMTS is 
currently under forbearance which mean s that the cellular operators are at 
liberty to offer various tariff options. Tariffs for CMTS have shown a 
continuously downward tren d in the recent past; this  is mainly due to the 
increased competition in the Cellular Sector. Cellular operators have various 
tariff plans with varying rates of monthly rental and airtime charges, which 
they go on revising from time to time. Information provided by TRAI 
indicates that currently there are more th an 600 different tariff plans available 
for the cellular subscribers across the country. 
(c) No, Sir. The rates of MTNL and BSNL are comparable and quite 
competitive as compared to the other operators. However, in view of the large 
number of different tariff plans across the country, it is not possible to make a 
meaningful comparison between the tari ffs charged for CMTS by the cellular 
operators and those charged by BSNL and MTNL for land line phones (under 
Basic Telephone Sen/ices). VSNL does not operate CMTS or Basic 
Telephone Service. 
SHRI BHAGATRAM MANHAR: Sir, the private cell operators are 
charging from Rs. 3,000 to Rs. 7,5000, as advance deposit, from subscribers 
for providing STD and ISD facilities. This is unjustified as crores of rupees 
are collected by cell operat ors for providing this service. In most of the 
advanced countries this practice is not adhered to. I would like to know from 
the hon. Minister whether he would di rect the TRAI to examine it and take 
positive actions in the interest of the consumers. 
SHRI ARUN SHOURIE: Sir, whethe r there will be large or small 
downpayments to be charged by the operator, it is to be determined 
completely by the market. In the TRAI's order on which there was a full 
discussion last time, in- the first half of the Session, as you know, they have 
given forbearance, that is, whatever am ount the persons want to charge, the 
operators want to charge and the cons umers are willing to pay, the cellular 
operators have that freedom in this regard. 
Now, I come to the issue of the consumers getting, agitated on this 
matter. Sir, they will walk away from the competition and go to 
20 

[10 April, 2003] RAJYA   SABHA 
some other provider - especially, I will be happy if they come to BSNL. But 
the more important point is that there is a procedure -laid down in the Act 
passed by the Parliament - which prescribes that if there is a group of 
consumers agitated about a particular method or aggrieved about a particular 
method, they can go to TDSAT for redressal. But if it is an individual 
consumer, he can go to the consumer  bodies set up under the Consumer 
Protection Act, 1988. 
SHRI BHAGATRAM MANHAR: Sir, my second supplementary is: 
Although the Government is committed to provide excellent service to 
consumers, recently, it has been noticed  that due to corporate rivalry,

operators, MTNL and BSNL to resolve all the pending issues of

SHRI ARUN SHOURIE: Sir, that is absolutely right. But it is corporate 
rivalry which has brought the rates down from Rs. 16.80 per minute to Rs. 
1.80 per minute. It is because of corporate rivalry. 
I come to the question of interconnectivity. You are right that in 
January this year, there was a problem. But as far as I know, there is no 
problem at the moment. That episode wh en they were not connecting calls of 
each other's networks is a matter that is now before TDSAT. TRAI itself has 
sent notices to all these people to explai n as to what happened at that time. 
But, if there is a specific complaint about interconnectivity, I would be 
delighted to look into it. 
SHRI RAJU PARMAR: Sir, the private cell phone operators have 
reduced the tariff and call charges dr astically during the last one year, 
although the cost of maintenance has remained unchanged. I would like to 
ask the hon. Minister the reasons for in creasing the rental and call charges as 
well as for reducing the pulse rate by MTNL and BSNL during the last one 
year. 
SHRI ARUN SHOURIE: Sir, as you kn ow, in the TRAI's order, it was 
prescribed that the rentals should be  increased. As I explained last time, 
BSNL and MTNL have given alternate packages to TRAI. 
21 

RAJYA SABHA [10 April, 2003] 
Due to the TRAI regulations. I am not in a position to disclose those 
packages, but you will find that the concerns expressed in this House by 
Members, both on monthly rentals and on pulse rates, have been addressed in 
those packages. If TRAI approves those packages, you will be very much 
satisfied with the result. Of course, this also means that the surplus of BSNL 
will be drastically reduced, because they used to finance the roll out to village 
telephony all by charging more on long distance telephony and those rates 
have collapsed as Mr. Parmar himself mentioned. If they do not increase 
rentals, they will have less surplus to roll out telephone services to the 
villages and for other things and then you will complain about it. 
In the next four years, BSNL requir es Rs. 29,000 crores for rolling out

Rs. 1 crore per year! That means for the four years, only Rs. 4 crores. So, we 
have to raise money from one place or the other. 
SHRIMATI S.G. INDIRA: Sir, when  the private cell operators come 
out with advertisements, they quote one rate and at the time of billing, they 
charge different rates. What steps is the TRAI going to take to ensure that the 
public is not taken for a ride by such companies? 
SHRI ARUN SHOURIE: Sir, as I have explained in my answer, there 
are 600 different packages in  the market that are available to the subscribers. 
There are 600 different types of rate arrangements. So, a consumer may be

package. If there is any specific comp laint which the service provider does 
not attend to, as I have explained to you, it is either the Consumer Court 
which will look into it or if there is a group of consumers that is aggrieved, it 
will be taken care of by the TDSAT.

Conduct of WLL Players 
*415. SHRI ABANI ROY: Will the Minister of COMMUNICATION 
AND INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY be p.eased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that as per Cellular Operators Association of 
India, WLL companies are misleading the public; 
(b) if so, whether the COAI has urged Government and TRAI to check 
role of the players of WLL who are cheating the public; 
(c) if so, the details thereof; and 
(d) the concrete plans formulated to check the role of the WLL 
players? 
THE MINISTER OF COMMUNICATIONS AND INFORMATION 
TECHNOLOGY (SHRI ARUN SHOURIE): (a) to (d) A Statement is laid on 
the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) to (d) Cellular Operators Association of India (COAI) had 
complained to Government and Telecom Regulatory Authority of India 
(TRAI) that one basic service operator is indulging in mis-informing public 
by giving full page advertisements in national dailies proclaiming that they 
will be offering free all India roaming. Also that another basic service 
operator is providing limited mobilit y facility beyond its licensed service 
area of Delhi. 
Telecom Regulatory Authority of India (TRAI) sought comments of M/s. 
Tata Teleservices Ltd. and M/s. Reliance Infocom Ltd. TRAI has thereafter 
noted that M/s. Tata Teleservices Ltd. are making efforts to control the radio 
frequency spillage beyond Delhi Short Distance Charging Area (SDCA) and they 
will be constantly monitoring the situation to control and minimize the radio 
frequency spillage. TRAI has further emphasized that M/s. Tata Teleservices 
should offer WLL (MOBILE) service within the SDCA area. M/s. Reliance 
Infocom Ltd. responded by stating that they have stopped advertisments 
referring to roaming services. 
A meeting was held by the Government with the basic service 
operators and cellular mobile service operators in New Delhi on 14.2.2003. 
In the meeting, M/s. Reliance Infocom Ltd. informed that  the advertisement 
referring to roaming service will be withdrawn. Since then, no such 
advertisment has been reported.

Service operators to ensure service pr ovision within their service area in 
accordance with their respective licence conditions.

of MTNL is slightly on the higher side. The average fault rate per hundred per 
month in Delhi unit for the year 2002-03 (upto 31-01-2003) is 19.99, as 
against average of all Indian fault rate of 11.00 for the same period. 
Not only the Telecom network of Delhi is one of the oldest where paper 
core underground cables still exists but due to very fast development of basic 
infrastructure like construction of flyovers, widening of roads, digging by 
other utility services to maintain and meet growing demand of fast expanding 
population, there are more damages to  underground cables. However, the 
fault rate for the month of February, 2003 has been brought down to 17.27 
faults per 100 subscribers per month. 
(c) The steps taken to improve the telephone services of MTNL are 
given in the enclosed statement. 
Statement 
Steps taken to improve the telephone services of MTNL 
MTNL, Delhi has initiated several measures to reduce the fault rate as 
listed below: 
1. All the electro mechanical exchanges and analog electronic 
exchanges in MTNL, Delhi have be en replaced by digital electronic 
exchanges. 
86 

[10 April, 2003] RAJYA   SABHA 
2. Paper core underground cables ar e being replaced by Jelly filled 
cables/Optical fibre cables with Digital Loop Carriers (D.L.Cs.)- 
3. For higher capacity primary cables and junction cables, duct 
systems has been introduced. 
4. Rehabilitation work in respect of leading in cables and rewiring of 
multi storeyed building is being done. 
5. Overhead wires are minimized by introducing 5 pair cables and wall 
Distribution Points (DPs). 
6. The junction network has been completely transferred to optical 
fibre cable links. 
7. Further improvement is being done by providing Synchronous 
Digital Hierarchy (SDH) systems connected on the ring architecture. 
8. Subscriber loop length being reduced by planning more 
Remote Subscriber Units (RSUs)/R emote Line Units (RLUs)/Digital 
Loop Carriers (DLCs). 
9. Wireless technologies like Cordect, Wireless in Local Loop 
(WLL) have been introduced. Faults are monitored on daily basis by 
senior officers. 
10. Computerised fault reporting system is introduced, which helps in 
booking, testing and sending the faults to the concerned line staff. 
11. In addition to this, line staff is provided with pagers for easy 
communication and follow up with the testing staff for speedy clearance of 
faults. 
12. Managed leased Data Network system has been introduced to 
improve the performance of the leased circuits. 
13. MTNL has liberalized the policy to replace all telephone 
instruments older than 5 years or repaired more than 2 times. This is being 
implemented in phases. In the first phase, instruments more than eight years 
old are being replaced.
